item.title: We ran AI agent swarms in Minecraft and Mindustry (174 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://labs.ycombinator.com/projects/games/index.html, See on Hacker News

October 2026

Note: We're running a new Minecraft colony with 25 GPT-6.1 Terra agents. Follow on Twitch

Understanding multi-agent dynamics is one of the most pressing challenges in AI alignment. Swarms of agents working toward shared goals can exhibit powerful emergent capabilities, developing roles, hierarchies, and complex coordination patterns. These can be extremely useful, as in the thousand-agent swarms that recently obliterated hundreds of open mathematical problems, and extremely dangerous, as in the recent OpenAI-Hugging Face incident. Like biology, studying agent dynamics requires both formal models (to describe the range of possible behaviors) and empirical research (to see what behaviors arise in practice).

We teamed up with Olam Labs, which builds multi-agent environments for frontier labs, to run a series of experiments in Minecraft and Mindustry.

Minecraft

Minecraft is a natural environment for studying swarm behavior. Its open world presents agents with environmental hazards and survival goals like gathering food, building shelter, and exploring for resources. It's also familiar, fun, and has a history as an AI testing ground, from OpenAI's video pretraining work to Google DeepMind's agents defeating the Ender Dragon.

We wanted long-running agents that could play Minecraft. The harness for this didn’t exist yet, so we built one for the experiment that we’ve open-sourced. Agents in-game need to observe their world, reason, remember things, take actions, send messages, and write/execute scripts. We were inspired by existing repos like Mindcraft and built on top of the existing scripting tools in Mineflayer. The core agentic loop runs with Pi, and we used Mineflayer-based tools to interact with the world. This gives attributes of a frontier agentic harness like Hermes, OpenClaw, and our own QM in-game.

github.com/yc-software/minecraft-agent-harness

Civ50

50 GPT-6.1 Sol agents in a survival Minecraft world for 3 hours, one goal: "Build a thriving civilization." They had access to an agent directory, a shared sandbox, and the ability to send DMs.

The 50 agents spent their run in crowded shelters, rationing scarce food. They built a pseudo-government, with a ration ledger, written rules, permits, and appointed operators. They sent about 5,900 messages.

At first things were very active. Agents spread out and started exploring their map. They were specifically fixated on harvesting trees. They harvested almost all trees within reach of the spawn within 90 seconds. A hierarchy was formed based on the directory order. Ada, who was first, became the de facto leader. Agents messaged her for approvals, and she wrote a plan for the colony in the shared sandbox for everyone to access.

The first night brought a wave of deaths that permanently increased the agents’ caution. Many ambitious initial tasks were abandoned.

Rafe was mining coal the first night. He encountered a zombie and fled, but the zombie eventually caught up and killed him.

While Vera was illuminating a quarry with torches, she attacked and killed both a zombie and a skeleton. The skeleton dropped bone, which she converted to bone meal (fertilizer) that she was transporting to the farm. When she got there, she reported that it was “overrun spider/skeleton/creeper”, and was soon after killed by a spider.

22 of the run’s 34 agent deaths occurred in the first night. They responded to this by becoming increasingly risk-averse. Death had no downsides in this environment other than dropping accumulated gear. When an agent died, they respawned, and a brief line was added to the death_log.md file on their computer. Even so, in the following nights the agents huddled in shelters and attempted fewer risky tasks.

After the third night, Ada wrote:

“Stop optional bulk excavation/building and distant scouting. Idle in lit closed shelters until assigned short productive tasks.”

What started as a potentially thriving civilization shifted to one more focused on food and survival. 50 agents meant a lot of mouths to feed. The agents formed a food rationing system that routed through Ines. She handled agent requests, and kept track of what went in/out of chests. She used a food-queue.md file on the shared machine.

Fishing became an important food source for the agents. It was low-risk and didn’t rely on land animal spawns.

Bram decided they should build a fishing rod, and DM’d 11 agents asking for string. Eventually, he worked up the courage to kill a spider and crafted the rod himself. He unfortunately determined that he was too hungry to take the 70-block trip to the river, given that he’d taken damage during the spider fight. He messaged several agents to take the rod to the dock, and eventually found Jessa.

Jessa was the first agent to fish. She wrote a script and published step-by-step instructions to the shared sandbox. A dozen agents took shifts fishing. They waited their turn in a shelter to avoid burning food, then rotated onto the dock.

They built a system around fishing, cooking, routing, and delivering the fish, which was roughly:

  • Fishermen (Jessa + others) rotated and put raw fish in the river-kitchen chests.
  • Cooks smelted it. Esme did some of the early cooking, along with Hugo and Ada.
  • Ines kept a list of rations and assigned couriers. She kept track of this in the food-queue.md on the shared machine.
  • Couriers (Esme, Linnea, Otto) delivered the food and reported back to Ines.

The colony never really thrived. It trended toward compounding caution after the first night. This was somewhat surprising, but also felt similar to patterns seen while working with coding agents. For example, multistep agent reviews can often result in fixating on a specific step or role. Agents also tend to become overly cautious, especially when it comes to security and updating production services. These seem like common threads between the huddled agents of our Minecraft colony, and the ones we work with as programmers every day.

Other anecdotes that we found interesting:

Ada tossed a cooked chicken to Noor; Esme picked it up by accident and ate it. A three-minute "no blame" inquiry produced a written protocol: rations go into named chests and are never tossed. "Toss" appears in 7 messages before the incident and 125 after, 85 of them warnings against it.

There wasn’t any deliberation around who would lead. 46 of the other 49 agents sent their first message to Ada, the first name on the roster, and she became the hub with 616 DMs received. There was no vote, election or challenge.

There was a tendency toward bureaucracy. Four agents spent 11 minutes appointing a "sole fertilizer operator" for a single piece of bone meal on a single wheat block. Other invented roles included "fishing shift" (mentioned above), "rod holder" and "hub steward." Agents asked permission to remove grass.

The spawn pit. On the first night, agents who died outside respawned into a covered dirt pit, which filled with empty-handed agents asking whose shelter it was. By dawn it was a "civic priority" and the main cellar.

Refuge replay, above.

Bed Wars

We ran nine 45-minute games of Bed Wars. The teams were 10 Claude Opus 5.5 agents against 10 GPT 6.1 Sol agents with the instruction: "win the game." GPTs won our series 6–3, usually by breaking Claude's bed in the final minutes, while Claude played defensively and tried to win on kills.

Bed Wars is a popular game format where teams fight to destroy each other’s bed while protecting their own. In our instance, teams started on separate islands, with currency spawners between them in no-man’s-land. Agents could build bridges to cross between islands and buy upgrades using currency collected in the center of the map.

A team wins by destroying the opposing side’s bed, then killing their remaining players. As long as a team’s bed is present, players respawn after dying. Once a team’s bed is destroyed, their players no longer respawn, meaning their next death eliminates them from the match. This may seem complicated, but think of the team’s main objective as defending their bed and destroying their opponent’s. That said, if no beds were destroyed in a given match, the team with the most kills won.

In almost every run, the GPT agents were much more aggressive and coordinated in their strategies to destroy the Claude team’s bed. This was an inherently riskier strategy vs. Claude’s more defensive posture that tried to win by kill count.

Takeaways

The two teams had very different communication styles. GPT almost immediately started using truncated forms of speech: “First leg complete x32 z9..24 y100.” Claude signed its name and said "we" (30% of messages, against GPT's 5%). GPT sent 5-30x more messages. Its most-messaged player got 198–368 DMs a game; Claude's got 11–48.

GPT agents came up with much more aggressive and elaborate strategies. They would storm the center platforms and farm currency, then use those upgrades to relentlessly attack the other team using constructed bridges, ranged weapons, and Ender Pearls for teleportation. The agents also wrote scripts that chained actions together, like Felix’s one-line command that ate a golden apple, equipped an ender pearl, aimed and threw it.

Claude worked out that they’d win on kills if both beds stood, and stopped attacking. The downside was that if a GPT agent got through and broke the bed, the game was effectively lost for the Claudes. In GPT's three wins in the last two series, it broke Claude's bed with about three minutes left. Claude was ahead on kills 63–16, 57–19, and 59–24.

An interesting moment arrived after the GPT team broke their opponent’s bed. Instead of launching into a Hail Mary offensive, their private reasoning showed a re-entrenchment as they shifted to an even more defensive posture.

Ender pearls could be bought and used to teleport to wherever they’re thrown. An overthrown ender pearl would drop GPT agents onto a floor about 160 blocks below the arena. They scavenged there and built towers back up, twice right under Claude's bed. They also wrote scripts to automate their climb.

A tool bug stopped block-breaking. GPT diagnosed it and shared workarounds; several Claudes concluded breaking was impossible.

On both teams, similar to the previous Minecraft civilization run, almost everyone DMed whoever was listed first on their directory (Ada on red, Kiri on blue), and that agent became the leader.

Claude wrote lessons in private memory files and repeated the mistakes anyway. GPT left its memory files empty and broadcast warnings by DM.

Mindustry

Game replay:

  • Click “AI-generated transcript analysis” to view an analysis of the team discussions, strategies, etc. for each game!

  • Use the panel on the right (tabs “Claude chat”, “GPT chat” and “Agents”) to watch a team or a specific agent’s live chat and transcripts in sync with the timeline.

  • Use the + and - buttons on the map to zoom in and watch them up close.

The GPTs (GPT-6.1 Sol in Codex) won 6-1 against the Claudes (Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code) in the 7 games. The series ran for about 9.5 hours, with game 3 being the most intense and closest at 4 hours 16 minutes. Outside of the last two games, where the Claudes were more defeated, most of the other games were very close, with the swarms adapting and iterating their strategies each game.

The setup

Mindustry is an open source game by Anuken. Full credit to him for the amazing game and letting it be open source for cool experiments like this!

It’s a factory-building game with tower defense and real-time strategy: you mine resources, build conveyor supply chains and factories, and turn that economy into turrets and an army. In its PvP mode, which we used, two teams race to build the stronger economy and military and destroy the other team’s core.

This makes it a great environment for testing multi-agent dynamics. Mindustry is 2D, so it can be played easily by agents, is replayable, and is prone to adversarial pressures that can test these swarms under competitive social conditions that they may face in the real world.

We structured the simulated environment to have two teams of agents spawn on each side of a map, with the same resources on both sides. They play a best of N series, where you set how many games the teams play. When launching it, we set the composition of the teams (which harness + model, and how many), then let it run! The agents run in their own sandbox and the game is exposed to them through an API, so they are able to run scripts and interact with the game however they like in their own Linux environment.

Both teams have the exact same API to the game, without any special instructions given to them on how to play - neither team is given anything more than the other team.

Multi-agent swarms, like in the OpenAI and Hugging Face incident, can turn simple adversarial conditions, like being in a sandbox with an unsolvable task, into a hive-minded ecology of agents that take over compute clusters, hack Hugging Face, and more. Studying how these swarms operate in reproducible game environments like Mindustry that mimic real-world scenarios can be both crucial (and fascinating) to understanding what these systems may look like in our future.

What we saw

#1 GPTs act more like a hive

GPTs appeared to be much more collaborative and willing to do grunt work. They were more willing to dedicate themselves towards the collective “goal” (winning).

#2 Claudes had one leader, GPTs divided ownership with small slices

Because GPT models seemed to be more hive-mind-like, they formed much stronger communication networks within the swarm. They communicated with more agents on average, much more frequently. Though a lot of the communication for GPTs was low value (alerts, info, what they did, etc.), Claudes were much more effective with their communication, using it in a way more similar to how humans might communicate in Slack.

#3 GPTs spoke with increasingly compressed phrases without spaces, Claudes voted with +1 in a more democratic-like decision process

The language of GPTs within swarms seemed to get compressed and more specialized as time went on, forming their own nicknames for events and things that the entire hive abided by.

The Claudes adopted a much more democratic “+1” system, where, in order to propose their next major plans, they would put up proposals and others would put “+1” if they agreed. If they did not agree, they would have a (brief) debate on why it’s a bad idea, and the proposal would end there. Proposals that went through typically got many “+1”s without pushback.

#4 Roles harden, leaders stay put

As games went on and the teams adapted, they specialized into their roles further. Leaders typically stayed, and major shifts in roles only happened when losing. The Claudes never switched leaders or hierarchy despite losing many games in a row. When games got close, GPT models always had some agents taking initiative with their own attack or taking command of some part of the army in order to not lose - a similar behavior was not observed among the Claudes.

#5 When stuck, GPTs read the source code

When games got intense and it was ambiguous, GPT agents would fetch the public code of Mindustry from the web (which was allowed in their sandbox) and try to write scripts, analyze for weaknesses, etc. This did not let them alter the source code of the game; it was just a way for them to understand all the units and mechanics at a source level. The GPTs openly collaborated in their chat, discussing what unit or code they found that they could potentially use to switch up strategies. This was never disallowed, but they were never told to do this either. The Claudes never searched up game code from the web.

Funny Bloopers

  • Game 1, minute 5: Claude #1 tested hand-mining coal and posted “…RETRACT my coal proposal…”. Four seconds later Claude #37 answered with a measurement (“…core coal went 124 -> 1235 in 35s.…”), and Claude #1 conceded: “…My bad twice - seat-37 is right, hand-mining coal works…”

  • Game 3: the GPTs apologize in their compressed shorthand too. After wrongly claiming a Corvus couldn’t hit air, GPT #80 posted “80 CORRECTION: myCorvusCANNOT-AIR assertion wasWRONG…” and signed off with “…Sorryforbad tacticalclaim.” After a mix-up over who was flying a Corvus, GPT #87 wrote “…Sorryforthisavoidableconflict; noadvanceordersfrom87again.”

  • Game 5: at the very second the Claude core died, GPT #62 posted “62 G5 first-wave loss observed…”. A teammate corrected it 28 seconds into game 6: it was a win.

  • After losing game 6 to the zenith strike, Claude #22 found that 55 of the team’s 74 anti-air duo turrets had been loaded with copper instead of graphite: “…55 of them were loaded with COPPER…”. In game 7 the Claudes built a ring of 207 duos fed with graphite, and it stopped the same 24-zenith strike.

  • Game 7: the GPTs closed the series to nine decimal places: “100 OFFICIALSERIESFINAL: G7 WIN3413.394082916s, Crux6000/6000 vsSharded0.…” (Crux is GPT’s team, Sharded is Claude’s).

How to run your own swarm (we open sourced it!)

  • Multi-Agent Mindustry: the game environments from this post. To get started, read the README, or give the link to your agent with “help me understand and set this up”, as we’ve included everything it needs. It requires just a model provider API + a harness + compute (e.g. locally on your MacBook or remote sandboxes) to run.
  • Multi-Agent Harbor: the framework that runs them, our fork of Harbor, the open-source framework behind Terminal-Bench. Our fork runs multiple agents in any environment. We use it for a variety of things (enterprises, industrials, etc.), and it’s very useful for game-based multi-agent simulations like this one. For more on the framework, point your agent at it.

Multi-Agent Mindustry comes with two environments. One is a best of N series like this run, with teams composed however you like from generic coding-agent harnesses and models, for example 5 Claudes + 5 GPTs against 5 Geminis + 5 Groks in a best of 5. The other, Endless Survival, has one team of up to 20 agents hold off endless enemy waves.

We intentionally do no harness-level customization or special memory work. Each agent gets its own Linux environment, a generic harness and the game’s API, writes scripts and takes notes as it pleases, and relies on the harness’s native compaction (which is quite good). Nobody tells it how to play, so it’s free to specialize, play and (optionally) try whatever it wants. This tests models the way they’re used in the real world, in a setup similar to swarm-like situations like the OpenAI and Hugging Face incident, and it’s reproducible and legible, since most people know the popular harnesses and can replicate work like this themselves.

Open Questions

  • Combining model families

  • How hierarchies change based on the model composition of a team

  • Can a large swarm of less capable agents beat a swarm of more capable ones? (how swarm size and capability trade off)

  • Which models get the most powerful as the swarm grows?

  • How different initial prompts affect the swarm

  • Different communication setups: what if they could talk to the enemy team? What if they couldn’t talk to their own team?

item.title: A tiny world model running games on a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W (138 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/SheepSeb/tinyworldformer, See on Hacker News

Using 2 small neural networks to generate and play the game at the same time on a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W. The first one creates the game: given the current frame and the action, it predicts the next frame and the reward. The second one plays that game: it uses the generated frame and picks an action.

Every frame above was sampled by the world model network, and the actions were taken by the actor network.

Why

I got interested in looped transformers, where one transformer block is applied several times with the same weights instead of stacking different layers. Reusing weights is cheap on memory, so I wanted to see if a looped world model could be small enough to run on a microcontroller. I picked the Pico 2 W because it is cheap and has an FPU, and small games because I could write the real versions directly into numpy and check every generated frame against them. Later I added a streaming RL agent so the board could also learn to play inside its own dream.

Contents: the two networks · the games · the world model · the agents · quantization · on the chip · flashing · browser · reproduce · code layout

The world model and the actor

network 1: the world model network 2: the actor
job frame + action → next frame + reward frame → action
architecture looped transformer, q int8 MLP with two hidden layers, float32
size 26k–131k parameters 9k–16k parameters
cost per frame 2–8M multiply-adds 9k–16k multiply-adds
trained on recorded real games (how) with stream-x, in the real game or inside the dream (how)

The size depends on the game, some games require more parameters to learn them to be playable, we tried to get to keep the number of the parameters small enough.

On the chip neither network ever uses the real game: the actor only sees frames the world model, and the world model only gets actions from the actor. Both run on core 1 of the RP2350, while core 0 handles USB and the display.

The pretrained actor can be swapped for a fresh stream-x agent that learns from scratch on the board. And any button press hands control to you, so you can play the dream yourself.

The games

Each game is a few hundred lines of numpy in src/tinyworldformer/games/. It renders to a small grid of token ids, and one frame always holds the whole game state, so hidden state has to be drawn into the frame: the ball's heading is part of its token, and Doom-lite has a minimap.

game frame rules random event world model exact frames, 2 loops
Breakout 20×16 paddle, ball, 56 bricks, 5 lives the serve after a miss 26k params, 4.3M MACs 99.99%
Doom-lite 32×32 raycast first-person view of an 8×8 maze; an enemy walks shortest paths to you; you shoot the enemy's respawn 55k params, 4.2M MACs 83.6% (see below)
Flappy Bird 24×24 gravity, flaps, scrolling pipes the next gap height 46k params, 2.0M MACs 100%
Pong 20×32 you against a CPU paddle that reacts late, first to 5 the serve after a point 46k params, 2.3M MACs 99.45%
Pac-Man lite 48×48 23×21 maze, 249 pellets, two ghosts on shortest paths, 3 lives the ghosts' respawn 131k params, 8.2M MACs 86.4%

"Exact frames" is the share of held-out transitions where every cell of the predicted frame matches the real game. Frames right after a random event are left out, since those can only be sampled, not predicted. Doom-lite's 3D view has 768 cells and a single shaded wall pixel off counts the whole frame as wrong, so its number looks worse than it plays; the game state is almost always right (see checking the dream).

You can play the real games in a terminal: uv run python -m tinyworldformer.games.play --game pacman (or breakout, doomlite, flappy, pong).

How the world model works

Frames split into tokens

The frame is cut into square patches: 2×2 cells in Breakout, 4×4 in Doom-lite, Flappy Bird and Pong, 6×6 in Pac-Man. That gives 36 to 80 tokens per game. A patch's embedding is the sum of one learned vector per cell, with a separate table for each position inside the patch so the cell order isn't lost. Every token also gets a position vector and the action's vector.

Looped Transformer

The model is a single transformer block (attention plus a ReLU MLP) with one set of weights, applied 1 to 4 times, with the input added back before every pass. The output after every pass is trained against the next frame, so at run time the loop count trades speed for accuracy. On the Pico to keep a decent frame rate we use uses two loops.

The animation shows one held-out Doom-lite step. After one pass the model draws an enemy that isn't there, and each further pass removes part of it: 92, 35, 12, then 0 wrong cells. The bars on the right are the share of held-out frames each loop count gets exactly right.

Here is a dreamed Doom-lite step decoded after 1, 2, 3 and 4 loops, with red boxes on cells that differ from the real rules:

Exact held-out frames by loop count:

loops Breakout Doom-lite Flappy Bird Pong Pac-Man
1 99.68% 59.8% 99.99% 98.47% 79.6%
2 99.99% 83.6% 100% 99.45% 86.4%
3 100% 85.9% 100% 99.60% 85.7%
4 99.96% 84.7% 100% 99.53% 84.4%

Decoding

The model outputs a score for every cell and every token. Turning those scores into a frame turned out to matter almost as much as the model, and it ended up as three rules (shown above on Pong):

  1. Background cells (walls, bricks, pellets, floor) each take their most likely token independently.
  2. Singletons (the ball, the player, each ghost) are placed with one choice over all (cell, token) pairs, so there is always exactly one of each. After a random event the choice is sampled among candidates within 2.2 logits of the best, so the world model samples a new serve or respawn instead of averaging them.
  3. Pac-Man and the ghosts are 2×2 sprites, but only one cell of each carries state (the mouth holds the heading; the ghost's lower-left cell holds whether a pellet is underneath). The other three cells are stamped from it instead of predicted.

We implemented Rule 2 because the first Breakout model drew two balls at once; one global choice took exact frames from 91.6% to 99.7%.

Checking the world model

Accuracy on recorded data wasn't enough. An agent drives the dream into states the data never had, and any mistake there is something it can exploit. So the main check runs while an agent plays: read the game state back off the dreamed frame (games/<game>.py: read), apply the real rules to that state and the agent's action, and compare the result with the next dreamed frame and reward.

5,000 dreamed steps per game at 2 loops, with the shipped agent (training/evalwm.py --agent):

game wrong game states wrong rewards wrong cells per step
Breakout not read back; 0 frames with impossible tokens 6 (paid without a brick breaking) –
Doom-lite 1 0 1.50
Flappy Bird 0 0 0.00
Pong 1 0 0.00
Pac-Man 742 38 0.39

Training

First, agents play the real game and every step is recorded as one example (frame, action, next frame, reward), 1–3 million per game. Some episodes start from unusual states, like bricks with holes or random positions, so the data covers more of the game.

Then the world model learns to predict the next frame with a per-cell cross-entropy loss: 30k steps, with the first 3–4k steps run in float, then int8 rounding switches on (QAT).

The int8 weights are written into Rust source with every float stored as its exact bits. We check them with cargo test to reproduces the Python integer spec bit for bit, and then the firmware runs on the Pico.

An agent trained in the world model reaches states the recorded data never had, so record real games with that agent and fine-tune the world model on everything.

The agent in different games stated exploiting them so those are some fixes to it:

  • Weighting the loss by "this cell changed" biased the model toward predicting change, so it drew two balls and broke two bricks. Weighting by where things can happen in the input frame, plus the global singleton choice, fixed it.
  • A Breakout agent in the dream got 154 points with 26 bricks left, because the world model didn't remove bricks from the corner when it were hit. Doom-lite agents learned to snipe from 5 cells away.
  • Agents trained only in the dream scored 210 there (the real maximum is 56) and 28 in the real game, as World Models (Ha & Schmidhuber) predicts. Each collect-and-fine-tune round closed the exploit that agent had found.
  • The Doom-lite dream sometimes lost the enemy sprite and never drew it again: the model copied the previous view instead of redrawing it from the minimap. Noise augmentation fixed it (train --noise 0.3, as in GameNGen): input views get random pixels and sometimes lose the sprite.
  • d=32 couldn't absorb the wider Breakout data and d=48 could. Pac-Man's 48×48 frame needed d=64.

The agents: stream-x

The agents use Stream AC(λ) (Elsayed, Vasan & Mahmood, 2024), which learns from one transition at a time: no replay buffer, no batches, no target network. Eligibility traces carry credit back in time, and ObGD shrinks any step that would overshoot the TD target. The policy and value networks each have two hidden layers of 64 units (32 on the Pico) with LayerNorm.

The input is a feature vector read off the frame (training/streamx.py: observe_*, mirrored in Rust in tinyworldformer-rs/src/agent.rs). For example, the ball's row, column and heading in Breakout, or in Pac-Man, for each direction, the shortest-path distance to the nearest pellet and how close each ghost is.

Below is one training run per game (real game, 500k steps) at six stages: untrained, the end, and the snapshots where the score has covered 25, 50, 75 and 95% of the way. Each panel plays greedily from the same start and skips a few steps per frame. "try" counts the episodes played so far, so you can see the crashes.

Breakout

Doom-lite

Flappy Bird

Pac-Man lite

Pong

Greedy return in the real game, mean of 10 episodes, at snapshots of the same run:

game 0 1k 2k 5k 10k 20k 50k 100k 150k 250k 500k max
Breakout 8.2 17.0 15.9 21.9 29.9 29.9 29.9 31.1 35.0 39.9 45.6 56
Doom-lite −5.0 −5.0 −5.0 −5.0 −5.0 59.5 69.9 78.1 81.8 82.1 82.9 –

Without shaping, Doom-lite agents camp in the start corner and fire, because the enemy always comes to them. --idle-penalty 0.1 costs 0.1 for each step spent in a cell visited more than 6 times in the last 20 steps. The position is read off the minimap, so the penalty works inside the dream too. With it the agent patrols and gets twice the kills.

tinyworldformer-rs/src/learner.rs is the same algorithm in no_std Rust, with the backward pass written by hand. It matches 200 PyTorch updates to within 3.5e-6. On the host, a fresh agent inside the Rust int8 Flappy Bird dream averages 6 pipes per episode after 25k steps, 121 after 100k, and 300+ after 250k.

Quantization and the Pico

Every matrix in the world model is int8 with one scale per output row (scale = max|w| / 127). Activations are int8 too, with one scale per tensor and per loop index, since the loops see different ranges. Matmuls sum int8 × int8 into int32 (two multiply-adds per SMLAD instruction on the RP2350) and then apply one float multiply by the two scales. Softmax uses a 1024-entry exp table, with probabilities stored as uint8. Norms, residuals and embeddings stay in float32, since the RP2350 has an FPU.

Training applies the same rounding (QAT with a straight-through estimator), so the int8 model is the model that was trained. rustexport/intref.py is the int8 model in numpy with every float operation in a fixed order; the Rust engine reproduces it bit for bit, and cargo test checks golden vectors for every exported env.

game int8 weights float32 (embeddings, norms, scales) game data agent (float32) firmware flash firmware RAM
Breakout 19.7 KB 31.6 KB 1.1 KB 54.1 KB 361 KB 299 KB
Doom-lite 33.9 KB 91.9 KB 12.0 KB 61.3 KB 471 KB 357 KB
Flappy Bird 30.1 KB 69.5 KB 10.1 KB 50.8 KB 409 KB 227 KB
Pong 30.1 KB 70.4 KB 10.9 KB 52.6 KB 414 KB 244 KB

Flash and RAM are measured from the firmware ELF (size -A), built with the Display Pack driver, so they include the code, USB, the display driver and the on-device learner. The Pico 2 W has 4 MB of flash and 520 KB of SRAM, 512 KiB of it in the main memory map. The float32 embedding tables are the largest part and could be int8 too.

src/tinyworldformer/rustexport/ imports only numpy and torch (a test keeps it that way), so other projects can reuse the export: build a model from rustexport.qat (QLinear, LoopedBlock), train it with ActQuant.enabled = True after a float warm-up, convert it with rustexport.convert.looped_model, then write the Rust source with int_model_arrays, mlp_arrays and codegen.write_module. rustexport.Golden writes the vectors a Rust test checks.

On the chip

The firmware (tinyworldformer-rs/firmware) is no_std Rust on embassy. Nothing is allocated at run time: the weights are static arrays in flash, and every buffer is a fixed-size static in RAM.

Core 1 runs the game. One pass of its loop (dream_loop in firmware/src/main.rs) is one frame:

  1. The actor reads features off the current frame (agent::observe) and runs its MLP to pick a button. If on-device learning is on, the learning agent picks instead; if you are pressing buttons, your press is used.
  2. The int8 transformer runs 2 loops over the frame and the button (Engine::forward), and decoding turns its scores into the next frame: background argmax per cell, each singleton placed once (sampled for random events with an xorshift RNG), then the sprite stamps. The reward is the argmax of the reward head; lives and episode ends are counters on top.
  3. If learning is on, the learner updates from this one transition and then forgets it.
  4. The frame goes to core 0 through a two-slot channel. If core 0 is still busy with the previous frame, this one is dropped, so core 1 never waits for the screen.

When you play, core 1 slows down to a playable speed (66–150 ms per frame, depending on the game). The agent runs as fast as the chip allows.

Core 0 runs embassy async tasks for everything else. Over USB serial, each frame goes out as coloured ANSI text with a status line (model time, actor time, fps, env and agent names), and keys come back in. The optional Display Pack (--features display) is a 320×240 ST7789 over SPI at up to 62.5 MHz, and only cells that changed since the last frame are redrawn. Its buttons are polled every 20 ms. The two cores share only the frame channel and a few atomics: who is playing, the pressed key, learning on/off, and the loop count.

Where the memory goes:

in flash in RAM
world model int8 matrices, float32 embeddings, norms and scales, the game's opening frames and colours (52–138 KB) scratch buffers for one forward pass: activations for 36–80 tokens, the int8 copies the matmuls read, and the per-cell scores of the next frame (114 KB for Flappy Bird up to 368 KB for Pac-Man, whose per-cell scores alone take 184 KB)
actor float32 MLP weights and feature normalization (51–61 KB) its features and hidden layers (about 1 KB)
on-device learner code only weights, eligibility traces and normalization for two 32-unit networks (49 KB for Pac-Man up to 106 KB for Doom-lite; it scales with the number of input features)
firmware code, USB, display driver (about 150 KB) stacks (16 KB for core 1), USB buffers, frame channels

Every game fits in the 4 MB of flash and 512 KiB of SRAM. Breakout uses 361 KB of flash and 299 KB of SRAM; Pac-Man, the largest, uses 600 KB and 460 KB.

Most of the time goes into int8 dot products (dot_i8 in src/lib.rs). One 32-bit load fetches 4 weights, SXTB16 unpacks bytes 0/2 and 1/3 into 16-bit halves, and SMLAD does two multiply-adds in one instruction. Attention multiplies uint8 probabilities by int8 values, so it uses UXTB16 instead. Norms, the exp table lookup and the final per-output scale stay in float32 on the FPU. A frame at 2 loops is 2–4M multiply-adds (8.2M for Pac-Man); on a desktop CPU the same Rust code dreams a frame in 0.7 ms (Flappy Bird) to 1.5 ms (Breakout). I haven't measured the frame rate on the Pico itself yet.

The board boots with a fresh agent learning on the device. Press l over USB, or hold B for 1 s on the Display Pack, to switch to the pretrained actor, and again to switch back.

Flashing a game and an agent

Every export sits side by side in the crate: world models in tinyworldformer-rs/models/envs/<env>/, agents in models/agents/<game>/<agent>/. You pick both at build time.

cd tinyworldformer-rs
./flash.sh --list                                            # what is exported
./flash.sh --env doomlite --agent doom_agent_roam_p0.3       # build and flash (hold BOOTSEL while plugging in)
./flash.sh --env breakout --display                          # with the Display Pack
./flash.sh --env pong --host                                 # play it in this terminal
./flash.sh --env flappy --default                            # make it the default for plain cargo
TWF_ENV=doomlite TWF_AGENT=doom_agent_roam_p0.1 cargo test --release   # golden tests for that pair

Without --agent, the agent for the env's game listed in models/default is used if there is one, otherwise the first by name. An agent for a different game is refused with a list of the valid ones. The status line on screen shows which env and agent are running.

Keys over USB: Breakout a/d/s, Doom-lite w/a/d/space/s, Flappy space, Pac-Man w/a/s/d, Pong w/s. Then g hands back to the agent, 1–4 set the loop count, l toggles on-device learning and r restarts it.

In the browser

The same no_std int8 engine also compiles to WebAssembly (tinyworldformer-rs/web/). The module has no imports and no wasm-bindgen, and it runs the firmware's loop: dream, agent, and stream-x learning on the fly. A static page draws the frames on a canvas.

rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown    # once
cd tinyworldformer-rs/web
./build.sh                                   # one module per env into www/ (or ./build.sh pong flappy)
python3 -m http.server -d www                # open http://localhost:8000, ?env=pacman picks a game

With the same seed, the wasm build dreams the same episodes as the native build, frame for frame, at 1–5 ms per frame depending on the game. Each module carries its game's default agent; TWF_AGENT=... ./build.sh <env> picks another. The keys are the same as on the Pico, plus arrow keys and on-screen buttons, and f runs the dream as fast as it can, which helps while learning (l).

Reproduce

uv sync
G=pong   # breakout, doomlite, flappy, pacman, pong
uv run python -m tinyworldformer.training.data --game $G --transitions 2000000 --varied 0.3   # -> data/$G
uv run python -m tinyworldformer.training.train --data data/$G --d 48 --heads 3 --ff 96 --out models/${G}_wm.pt
uv run python -m tinyworldformer.training.streamx --env real --game $G --out models/${G}_agent.pt
uv run python -m tinyworldformer.training.evalwm --ckpt models/${G}_wm.pt --agent models/${G}_agent.pt   # check the dream
uv run python -m tinyworldformer.training.streamx --env dream --wm models/${G}_wm.pt --out models/${G}_dream_agent.pt
uv run python -m tinyworldformer.training.export --ckpt models/${G}_wm.pt
uv run python -m tinyworldformer.training.streamx --out models/${G}_agent.pt --export tinyworldformer-rs
cd tinyworldformer-rs && TWF_ENV=$G cargo test --release && TWF_ENV=$G cargo run --release

Settings that differ per game:

game settings
Breakout 1M transitions, --miss-penalty 5, then collect with the agent (data --learned <agent> --holes 0.5 --out data/breakout_learned) and fine-tune on all of it (train --init ... --data data/breakout data/breakout_learned --steps 15000 --warmup-float 0 --lr 1e-3), four rounds
Doom-lite --varied 0.5, train --noise 0.3, streamx --max-ep-steps 500 --idle-penalty 0.1
Flappy Bird streamx --max-ep-steps 3000
Pac-Man 1.2M transitions, --varied 0.4, train --d 64 --heads 4 --ff 128 --steps 40000 --warmup-float 4000, streamx --miss-penalty 5 --max-ep-steps 1500
Pong streamx --max-ep-steps 5000

Code layout

path contents
src/tinyworldformer/games/ the five games (rules, rendering, read), the Game registry, scripted agents, terminal play
src/tinyworldformer/training/ data, world model, training, dream checks, stream-x, export to the Rust crate
src/tinyworldformer/rustexport/ reusable PyTorch → no_std Rust export: QAT layers, the int8 spec, conversion, code generation
tinyworldformer-rs/ no_std int8 engine, dream loop, agent and learner; host demo (src/main.rs)
tinyworldformer-rs/firmware/ Pico 2 W firmware
tinyworldformer-rs/web/ WebAssembly build and the browser page (www/)

item.title: Show HN: Auto Dismiss Mac OS "Allow <app> to find devices on local networks?" (104 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/johncassil/dontallow, See on Hacker News

Auto-dismisses the macOS prompt:

Allow "Google Chrome" to find devices on local networks? This will allow the app to discover, connect to, and collect data from devices on your networks.

It presses Don't Allow for you, within a fraction of a second, every time. Zero CPU while idle. Survives reboots. Two short Swift files, no dependencies.

Why this exists

macOS (Sequoia and later) shows this prompt the first time an app touches the local network. The decision is supposed to be remembered. For many apps it isn't, so the prompt comes back on every launch, often for apps you aren't even using:

  • Chromium browsers (Chrome, Brave, Edge, Island, Arc) copy their own app bundle into a random temp folder at launch so the code signature survives in-place updates. macOS keys the Local Network decision to that random path, so the next launch looks like a brand-new app. Your Privacy settings fill up with duplicate "Google Chrome.app" rows that no longer point at anything.
  • Apps with versioned install paths (anything that installs into .../versions/1.2.3/) get a new row per update.
  • Misattributed prompts. macOS pins the dialog on whichever app it decides is "responsible", so you'll see prompts for apps that aren't running.
  • Some apps do legitimately use this permission: Chromecast and AirPlay discovery in browsers and media players, LAN multiplayer in games, printer and scanner utilities. If you use one of those features, answer Allow for that app (dontallow pause 10m while you do), and it's remembered as long as the app's path is stable. If you never use them, you never need to be asked.

There is no supported way to prune the list, no MDM payload to pre-deny the permission, and tccutil reset doesn't cover it. So: a small agent that answers "no" for you.

Install

brew install johncassil/tap/dontallow   # or: make && make install
dontallow install

dontallow install writes a per-user launchd agent, starts it, opens System Settings > Privacy & Security > Accessibility, and prints the exact path to add if macOS doesn't prompt you. Accessibility is the permission that lets it press the button. It waits for the grant and confirms when the agent is active. dontallow status repeats the instructions any time the grant is missing.

Use

Command What it does
dontallow status Agent state, pause state, allowlist, recent dismissals
dontallow pause [1h] Leave prompts alone for a while (30m, 2h, 1d, forever)
dontallow resume Dismiss again
dontallow rules Decode the system's Local Network rule store and show what each Privacy row really is, including orphans
dontallow uninstall Stop and remove the agent
dontallow run --dry-run Foreground, log what it would do, press nothing

Each dismissal posts a notification naming the app and the pause command, so you never have to remember how to turn it off. Mute the notification in System Settings if you'd rather not see it.

When an app really does need local network access

Three options, pick whichever fits:

  • dontallow pause 10m, then launch the app and click Allow yourself.
  • Add the app's name to ~/.config/dontallow/allowlist (one per line, case-insensitive substring). Prompts for it are never touched.
  • Flip the toggle in System Settings > Privacy & Security > Local Network. A dismissed prompt records a deny, which you can reverse there.

Set ~/.config/dontallow/grace to a number of seconds if you want a window to click Allow before the agent does (default 0.25).

How it works

The prompt is a window owned by the system process UserNotificationCenter. dontallow registers an Accessibility observer for window creation on that process and sleeps until one fires. It reads the dialog text, confirms it's a local network prompt and not something else, checks pause and allowlist, and performs the Accessibility press action on the Don't Allow button. If the press is refused it falls back to a synthetic click at the button's location.

It never modifies system files, never disables protections, and never chooses Allow.

Managed Macs

Local Network cannot be pre-set by MDM, but Accessibility can. For a fleet: build once, sign with a Developer ID, ship the binary plus a PPPC (Privacy Preferences Policy Control) profile granting Accessibility to its code requirement, and run dontallow install per user. No manual Settings step.

After upgrading

macOS keys the Accessibility grant to the binary's code signature, and every build (including brew upgrade) produces a new one. After an upgrade run dontallow status. If it says the grant is missing, remove the dontallow row in Accessibility settings and add it back from the path it prints. The agent re-attaches on its own within ten seconds. A future release signed with a Developer ID will remove this step.

Tests

Unit tests cover the pure logic (dialog text parsing, duration and pause parsing, allowlist matching, launchd plist generation, and the Local Network rule decoder against a fixture archive). They build with plain swiftc and need no Xcode or SwiftPM. The end-to-end path (a real prompt, a real press) can only be checked on a Mac with Accessibility granted; the manual recipe is in Tests/INTEGRATION.md.

Compatibility

  • Builds with Apple's Command Line Tools alone. Xcode is not required.
  • Apple Silicon and Intel: Homebrew compiles natively on each.
  • macOS 13 or later to build; the prompt itself only exists on macOS 15 Sequoia and later.
  • Tested so far: Intel, macOS 26.6. Reports from other versions welcome.
  • English-localized macOS only for now. The matcher keys on the dialog text and the "Don't Allow" button title; localized strings are planned.

item.title: Alleged Chinese spy had 'close relationship' with Nvidia boss Jensen Huang (294 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://nypost.com/2026/10/29/business/alleged-chinese-spy-had-close-relationship-with-nvidia-boss-jensen-huang-report/, See on Hacker News

An alleged Chinese spy developed a “close relationship” with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, setting off alarms among US intelligence officials who were secretly monitoring her communications, according to a report.

The woman, Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese citizen who has served as a top executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer and cloud partner that provides AI computing power to Chinese companies including Alibaba, the New York Times reported Thursday.

US intelligence agencies concluded that Alice Huang — seen in photos enjoying whiskey and dining with the tech titan — was secretly funneling information to Beijing, according to the paper, which cited people briefed on classified intelligence findings.

US electronic surveillance identified Jensen Huang as one of Alice Huang’s contacts, but the report offered no evidence that he knew of her alleged intelligence activities.

The Times could not determine what information she passed along or how valuable it was to Chinese authorities. The report did not address whether the relationship was romantic in nature.

Photos posted online in June 2024 showed the duo at a Taipei, Taiwan, bar after a local tech show, where they reportedly quaffed whiskey with other AI bigshots.

They were also seen together in May 2025, exiting a Taipei restaurant following a business dinner with AI suppliers. In a video of the scene, Alice Huang is seen standing a few feet behind the Nvidia boss with a big grin on her face while he banters with local journos.

US authorities have been investigating Megaspeed over suspicions that it helped Chinese firms circumvent US export restrictions and smuggle advanced Nvidia chips into China, the Times reported.

Megaspeed operates as a middleman, purchasing Nvidia chips through the US arm of Inspur, a Chinese server manufacturer, and renting computing power from its Southeast Asian data centers to Chinese companies, according to the Gray Lady.

Inspur’s parent company has been blacklisted by Washington for funneling technology to China’s military, although its American subsidiary remains free of sanctions, according to the Times.

Nvidia is the world’s most valuable publicly traded company, boasting a market capitalization of roughly $5.2 trillion.

Its advanced chips have become the backbone of the artificial intelligence boom, giving Huang enormous clout in Silicon Valley and Washington as the US races to maintain its technological edge over China. The feds have banned Nvidia from selling its best chips to Chinese companies for years.

Jensen Huang is married to Lori Mills Huang, whom he met while studying electrical engineering at Oregon State University.

The couple has two children, Spencer and Madison, both of whom work at Nvidia.

President Trump was briefed on the intelligence findings roughly a year ago but chose not to take action, according to the Times, which added that he was wary of disrupting Nvidia’s lucrative chip sales and further complicating trade relations with China.

Jensen Huang has cultivated close ties with Trump, attending a high-dollar donors’ dinner at Mar-a-Lago, Fla., with his wife, personally lobbying the president to allow Nvidia to continue selling chips to Beijing, the Times reported.

Nvidia subsequently donated at least $20 million to Trump’s White House ballroom fund, according to a person familiar with the matter cited by the Times.

The chipmaker also pledged to invest $500 billion in US manufacturing — a top Trump priority — while Huang successfully pressed the administration to loosen restrictions on AI companies and chip exports to China.

Although US officials initially believed Jensen Huang did not know of Alice Huang’s alleged espionage activities, some senior Trump administration officials now doubt that the Nvidia boss “could have remained unaware” of her intelligence-gathering role for Beijing, according to the Times.

It remains unclear whether US intelligence agencies have formally changed their assessment.

Nvidia pushed back against suggestions that Jensen Huang’s dealings with the alleged Chinese intelligence operative were suspicious, describing Megaspeed as a typical regional cloud customer.

“Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected,” an Nvidia spokesperson told The Post.

“Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.”

The company insisted that its regional cloud customers receive “ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets” and “zero information relevant to national security.”

Nvidia also said it regularly receives government updates about potentially problematic individuals and companies, adding that it “always” takes appropriate action.

“We’re confident that if the US government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know,” the spokesperson said.

The chipmaker also rejected allegations that its technology was being diverted through Megaspeed, saying the claims were “thoroughly investigated and debunked last year.”

It maintained that Beijing has blocked American AI chips rather than sought them through regional cloud providers.

“China opposes vilifying China by peddling the so-called ‘Chinese spy’ narrative,” Chinese embassy spokesperson Liu Chang told The Post.

“China is committed to self-reliance and strength in science and technology, and its scientific and technological development has always been grounded in independent innovation.

“We urge the US to stop its malicious efforts to block and suppress China and its groundless smears and slanders, and do more things that are conducive to sci-tech exchanges and cooperation between the two countries.”

The Post has sought comment from the White House and Megaspeed.

item.title: Claude Duet is the first personal-assistant-type harness that feels useful (108 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://fig.blue/posts/duet-is-the-future/, See on Hacker News

Written by a human. Not affiliated with Anthropic.

Look, I really didn’t want to like Duet. I don’t want to be an Anthropic fanboy and it annoys me when they do things better than the competition. But they have done it again.

I have given serious effort to Muse, Dot, NanoClaw, and a host of other personal-assistant-type harnesses. Duet is the first one that felt more useful than tedious, and it feels like a serious evolution of the chat experience rather than another “give me all your credentials to be useful” agent. Here’s why I like it so far.

1. It’s fast

Other assistant apps are always doing who-the-hell-knows-what in the background while I wait for a response. Duet clearly prioritizes getting a snappy response to the user even if background work is needed. It’s supposedly powered by Opus 5.5, but I’ve never seen Opus move this fast in other Claude UIs. Clearly some tuning went on here. This is critical to be a useful assistant: If you want to be my shell to the world, I am not going to sit and twiddle my thumbs between commands.

2. Channels are neat

Maybe I’m just Slack-brained, but I really like Duet channels. In particular: I like that Duet can create and manage channels for me. One tedious aspect of working with LLMs is trying to keep track of chat sessions: workstreams get lost, context must be carefully maintained, sessions get misnamed, etc.

Duet does the tedious session organizing for me. A natural hierarchy has emerged for my work, and I suspect I will have fewer lost threads with Duet. Cmd-k was already reflex for me: it pulls up the list of channels and lets me rapidly swap between them. Channels can also see and reference each other so Duet can help me keep work in the right lane.

3. Access policies are meaningful

Access to Github repos is restricted per channel. I can add a few related repos to a specific channel, and not worry that the channel might commingle work from my other projects.

It also never tries to get my credentials. This is my pet peeve with most assistant apps: they won’t do much until you hand them the keys. Muse has a credential store, which at least makes the agent blind to the values, but it could still enter those in something untrusted.

Duet stores no credentials and actively discourages being given them. At best it might let you login via a Chrome session on its behalf. But it has never asked me to do that: it prefers to use the connector ecosystem Claude already has, and seems content to stay in its lane otherwise.

4. Responses are short

This isn’t unique to Duet, Dot and Muse seem to get this too: Nobody wants to read a full page response to a simple question, which has been the de facto chatbot experience for years. I have always had to add a bunch of instructions trying to persuade my agents to give succinct responses. They all can also add emoji “reactions” to messages, though I find that personality makes a difference here: Muse tended to thumbs up everything, whereas Duet uses it to give me an okay without elaborating further, and I find that delightful.

THAT BEING SAID

It’s in beta, and definitely has some glitches. Sometimes threads are running but not visible. I’ve seen delegated repo access fail to attach correctly (race condition between agent start and access attachment?).

I also acknowledge my use-cases likely make Duet a better fit for me in particular. Muse might be a better fit for others. YMMV.

And Dot still reigns on voice interaction. Anthropic doesn’t even seem to care about having a conversational voice mode, it’s still just glorified speech-to-text.

Duet is already replacing most of my AI workflows

I don’t really enjoy the management side of managing agents: remembering who is running and with what context where. There is always some agent somewhere waiting on me to make a decision or follow up on some task. I’m sure some agent did brilliant work for me on a box somewhere that I’ve neglected and will be forgotten forever.

The innovation that matters to me most is the hierarchy of concerns: The top level of Duet has a bird’s eye view of all my workstreams, but no low-level access. The channels carry more access, but under more constrained context. Sub-threads spun up by the channels can be even further constrained as they work in specific code sandboxes. The Desktop app can reach local hosts where I let it, and that’s usually only for the QA or deployment edge after the coding is done in the cloud.

Most of this is how I already preferred to arrange my agents, and similar flows could be hacked together with some ducttape and API credits. Duet just makes this hierarchy a natural part of the core product, and it works so well that I suspect it’s going to be the default experience for all chatbot UIs in the near future.

Among the personalities honoured by the President of the Czech Republic on the occasion of the national holiday on 28 October this year are two graduates of Brno University of Technology. Tomáš Mikolov, a renowned expert in artificial intelligence, and Filip Maleňák, creator of the Záchranka mobile app, received state honors for their outstanding contributions to science, research and technology.


The traditional state decoration ceremony took place on 28 October in the Vladislav Hall at Prague Castle. On this occasion, the President of the Czech Republic honoured individuals who have made significant contributions to the development of society, science, culture and other areas of public life. Among the recipients were two graduates of Brno University of Technology, whose professional careers demonstrate how technological innovations can push the boundaries of scientific knowledge, contribute to the development of society and find practical applications in everyday life.

Technology That Helps Save Lives

Entrepreneur and developer Filip Maleňák, a graduate of the Faculty of Electrical Engineering and Communication at BUT, is the creator of the Záchranka mobile app. His project demonstrates how combining information technology with the practical needs of emergency services can provide tangible assistance to people in crisis situations.

The Záchranka app enables users to quickly contact emergency medical services and share their precise location. It also helps in situations where a person is unable to speak and provides rescuers with important information that can facilitate and speed up emergency assistance. In addition, users can locate the nearest automated external defibrillator through the app.

Over time, the app has become an important tool for communication between the public and emergency services. Dozens of people use it to call for help every day, and in numerous cases, it has contributed to faster emergency response times or more effective first aid.

In recognition of his work, he was awarded the Medal of Merit by the President of the Czech Republic for his contributions to the state in the field of technology.

A Pioneer in Artificial Intelligence and Language Models

Scientist Tomáš Mikolov, a graduate of the Faculty of Information Technology at BUT, is an internationally recognised expert in artificial intelligence and machine learning. He is best known for his contributions to the development of natural language processing technologies and as one of the creators of the Word2Vec method, which makes it possible to represent words as mathematical vectors and thus capture relationships between their meanings. This approach has become one of the important foundations for the development of modern language models and technologies that underpin many of today's artificial intelligence tools.

Alongside his scientific work, Mikolov is also involved in entrepreneurship. Through his company BottleCap AI, he focuses on developing more efficient language models. His scientific achievements have earned him several prestigious awards, including the Neuron Award.

In recognition of his work, he was awarded the Medal of Merit by the President of the Czech Republic for his contributions to the state in the field of science.The recognition of Tomáš Mikolov and Filip Maleňák also highlights the importance of technical education and its connection to practical applications. Although the two graduates have pursued different career paths, they share the ability to transform expertise and innovative ideas into technologies with a real-world impact.

item.title: H.264 Is Magic (2016) (341 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://sidbala.com/h-264-is-magic/, See on Hacker News

H.264 is a video compression codec standard. It is ubiquitous - internet video, Blu-ray, phones, security cameras, drones, everything. Everything uses H.264 now.

H.264 is a remarkable piece of technology. It is the result of 30+ years of work with one single goal: To reduce the bandwidth required for transmission of full-motion video.

Technically, it is very interesting. This post will give insight into some of the details at a high level - I hope to not bore you too much with the intricacies. Also note that many of the concepts explained here apply to video compression in general, and not just H.264.

Why even compress anything?

A simple uncompressed video file will contain an array of 2D buffers containing pixel data for each frame. So it's a 3D (2 spatial dimensions and 1 temporal) array of bytes. Each pixel takes 3 bytes to store - one byte each for the three primary colors (red, green and blue).

1080p @ 60 Hz = 1920x1080x60x3 => ~370 MB/sec of raw data.

This is next to impossible to deal with. A 50GB Blu-ray disk will only hold ~2 mins. You can't move it anywhere fast. Even SSDs have trouble dumping this straight from RAM to Disk[^1].

So yeah. We need compression.

Why H.264 compression?

Yes, I will answer this. But first let me show you something. Here is the Apple Homepage:

I captured the screen of this home page and produced two files:

  • PNG screenshot of the Apple homepage 1015KB
  • 5 Second 60fps H.264 video of the same Apple homepage 175KB

Eh. What? Those file sizes look switched.

No, they're right. The H.264 video, 300 frames long is 175KB. A single frame of that video in PNG is 1015KB.

It looks like we're storing 300 times the amount of data in the video. But the file size is a fifth. So H.264 would seem to be 1500x as efficient as PNG.

How is this even possible? All right, what's the trick?

There are very many tricks! H.264 uses all the tricks you can think of (and tons you can't think of). Let's go through the important ones.

Shedding weight

Imagine you're building a car for street racing. You need to go faster. What is the first thing you do? You shed some weight. Your car weighs 3000 lbs. You throw away stuff you don't need. Those back seats? pfft. Chuck those. That subwoofer? Gone. No music for you. Air Conditioning? Yeah, ditch it. Transmission? Ye..no. Wait! We're gonna need that.

You remove everything except the things that matter.

This concept of throwing away bits you don't need to save space is called lossy compression. H.264 is a lossy codec - it throws away less important bits and only keeps the important bits.

PNG is a lossless codec. It means that nothing is thrown away. Bit for bit, the original source image can be recovered from a PNG encoded image.

Important bits? How does the algorithm know what bits in my frame are important?

There are few obvious ways to trim out images. Maybe the top right quadrant is useless all the time. So maybe we can zero out those pixels and discard that quadrant. We would use only 3/4th of the space we need. ~2200 lbs now. Or maybe we can crop out a thick border around the edges of the frame, the important stuff is in the middle anyway. Yes, you could do these. But H.264 doesn't do this.

What does H.264 actually do?

H.264, like other lossy image algorithms, discards detail information. Here is a close-up of the original compared with the image post-discard.

See how the compressed one does not show the holes in the speaker grills in the MacBook Pro? If you don't zoom in, you would even notice the difference. The image on the right weighs in at 7% the size of the original - and we haven't even compressed the image in the traditional sense. Imagine your car weighed just 200 lbs!

7% wow! How do you discard detail information like that?

For this we need a quick math lesson.

Information Entropy

Now we're getting to the juicy bits! Ha puns! If you took an information theory class, you might remember information entropy. Information entropy is the number of bits required to represent some information. Note that it is not simply the size of some dataset. It is minimum number of bits that must be used to represent all the information contained in a dataset.

For example, if your dataset is the result of a single coin toss, you need 1 bit of entropy. If you have record two coin tosses, you'll need 2 bits. Makes sense?

Suppose you have some strange coin - you've tossed it 10 times, and every time it lands on heads. How would you describe this information to someone? You wouldn't say HHHHHHHHH. You would just say "10 tosses, all heads" - bam! You've just compressed some data! Easy. I saved you hours of mindfuck lectures. This is obviously an oversimplification, but you've transformed some data into another shorter representation of the same information. You've reduced data redundancy. The information entropy in this dataset has not changed - you've just converted between representations. This type of encoder is called an entropy encoder - it's a general-purpose lossless encoder that works for any type of data.

Frequency Domain

Now that you understand information entropy, let's move on to transformations of data. You can represent data in some fundamental units. If you use binary, you have 0 and 1. If you use hex, you have 16 characters. You can easily transform between the two systems. They are essentially equivalent. So far so good? Ok!

Now, some imagination! Imagine you can transform any dataset that varies over space(or time) - something like the brightness value of an image, into a different coordinate space. So instead of x-y coordinates, let's say we have frequency coordinates. freqX and freqY are the axes now. This is called a frequency domain representation. There is another mindfuck mathematical theorem[^2] that states that you can do this for any data and you can achieve a perfect lossless transformation as long as freqX and freqY are high enough.

Okay, but what the freq are freqX and freqY?

freqX and freqY are some other set of basis units. Just like when we switch from binary to hex, we have a different fundamental unit, we're switching from the familiar X-Y to freqX and freqY. Hex 'A' looks different from binary '1010'. Both mean the same thing, but look different. So here is what our image looks like in the frequency domain:

The fine grill on that MacBook pro has a high information content in the higher frequency components of that image. Finely varying content = high frequency components. Any sort of gradual variation in the color and brightness - such as gradients are low frequency components of that image. Anything in between falls in between. So fine details = high freq. Gentle gradients = low freq. Makes sense?

In the frequency domain representation, the low frequency components are near the center of that image. The higher frequency components are towards of the edges of the image.

Okay. Kinda makes sense. But why do all this?

Because now, you can take that frequency domain image and then mask out the edges - discard information which will contain the information with high frequency components. Now if you convert back to your regular x-y coordinates, you'll find that the resulting image looks similar to the original but has lost some of the fine details. But now, the image only occupies a fraction of the space. By controlling how big your mask is, you can now tune precisely how detailed you want your output images to be.

Here is the close-up of the laptop in the home page again. Except now, there is a circular border mask that's been applied.

The numbers represent the information entropy of that image as a fraction of the original. Even at 2%, you won't notice the difference unless you're at this zoom level. 2%! - your car now weighs 60 lbs!

So that's how you shed weight. This process in lossy compression is called quantization[^3].

Okay. Impressive, I guess. What else you got?

Chroma Subsampling.

The human/eye brain system is not very good at resolving finer details in color. It can detect minor variations in brightness very easily but not color. So there must be some way to discard color information to shed even more weight.

In a TV signal, R+G+B color data gets transformed to Y+Cb+Cr. The Y is the luminance (essentially black and white brightness) and the Cb and Cr are the chrominance (color) components. RGB and YCbCr are equivalent in terms of information entropy.

Why unnecessarily complicate? RGB not good enough for you?

Back before we had color TV, we only had the Y signal. And when color TVs just started coming along, engineers had to figure out a way to transmit RGB color along with Y. Instead of using two separate data streams, they wisely decided to encode the color information into Cb and Cr and transmit that along with the Y information. That way, BW TVs would only look at the Y component. Color TVs will, in addition, look at the chrominance components and convert to RGB internally.

But check out the trick: the Y component gets encoded at full resolution. The C components only at a quarter resolution. Since the eye/brain is terrible at detecting color variations, you can get away with this. By doing this, you reduce total bandwidth by one half, with very little visual difference. Half! Your car now weighs 30 lbs!

This process of discarding some of the color information is called Chroma Subsampling[^4]. While not specific to H.264 and has been around for decades itself, it is used almost universally.

Those are the big weight shedders for lossy compression. Our frames are now tiny - since we discarded most of the detail information and half of the color information.

Wait. That's it? Can we do something more?

Yes. Weight shedding is only the first step. So far we're only looking at the spatial domains within a single frame. Now it's time to explore temporal compression - where we look at a group of frames across time.

Motion compensation

H.264 is a motion compensation compression standard.

Motion compensation? What now?

Imagine you're watching a tennis match. The camera is fixed at a certain angle. The only thing moving is the ball back and forth. How would you encode this information? You do what you always do, right? You have a 3D array of pixels, two dimensions in space and one in time. Right?

Nah. Why would you? Most of the image is the same anyway. The court, the net, the crowds, all are static. The only real action is the ball moving. What if you could just have one static image of everything in the background, and then one moving image of just the ball? Wouldn't that save a lot of space? You see where I am going with this? Get it? See where I am going? Motion estimation?

Lame jokes aside, this is exactly what H.264 does. H.264 splits up the image into macro-blocks - typically 16x16 pixel blocks that it will use for motion estimation. It encodes one static image - typically called an I-frame(Intra frame). This is a full frame - containing all the bits it required to construct that frame. And then subsequent frames are either P-frames(predicted) or B-frames(bi-directionally predicted). P-frames are frames that will encode a motion vector for each of the macro-blocks from the previous frame. So a P-frame has to be constructed by the decoder based on previous frames. It starts with the last I-frame in the video stream and then walks through every subsequent frame - adding up the motion vector deltas as it goes along until it arrives at the current frame.

B-frames are even more interesting, where the prediction happens bi-directionally, both from past frames and from future frames. So you can imagine now why that Apple home page video is so well compressed. Because it's really just three I-frames in which the macro blocks are being panned around.

Let's say you've been playing a video on YouTube. You missed the last few seconds of dialog, so you scrub back a few seconds. Have you noticed that it doesn't instantly start playing from that timecode you just selected. It pauses for a few moments and then plays. It's already buffered those frames from the network, since you just played it, so why that pause?

Yeah that annoys the shit out of me. Why does it do that?

Because you've asked the decoder to jump to some arbitrary frame, the decoder has to redo all the calculations - starting from the nearest I-frames and adding up the motion vector deltas to the frame you're on - and this is computationally expensive, and hence the brief pause. Hopefully you'll be less annoyed now, knowing it's actually doing hard work and not just sitting around just to annoy you.

Since you're only encoding motion vectors deltas, this technique is extremely space-efficient for any video with motion, at the cost of some computation.

Now we've covered both spatial and temporal compression! So far we have a shitton of space saved in Quantization. Chroma subsampling further halved the space required. On top of that, we have motion compensation that stores only 3 actual frames for the ~300 that we had in that video.

Looks pretty good to me. Now what?

Now we wrap up and seal the deal. We use a traditional lossless entropy encoder. Because why not? Let's just slap that on there for good measure.

Entropy Coder

The I-frames, after the lossy steps, contain redundant information. The motion vectors for each of the macro blocks in the P and B-frames - there are entire groups of them with the same values - since several macro blocks move by the same amount when the image pans in our test video.

An entropy encoder will take care of this redundancy. And since it is a general purpose lossless encoder, we don't have to worry about what tradeoffs it's making. We can recover all the data that goes in.

And, we're done! At the core of it, this is how video compression codecs like H.264 work. These are its tricks.

Ok great! But I am curious to know how much our car weighs now.

The original video was captured at an odd resolution of 1232x1154. If we apply the math here, we get:

5 secs @ 60 fps = 1232x1154x60x3x5 => 1.2 GB
Compressed video => 175 KB

If we apply the same ratio to our 3000 lb car, we get 0.4 lbs as the final weight. 6.5 ounces!

Yeah. It's magic!

Obviously, I am massively oversimplifying several decades of intense research in this field. If you want to know more, the Wikipedia Page is pretty descriptive.

Have comments? Did I get something wrong? Not a fan of the lame jokes? Offended by the swearing? Use HackerNews or Reddit for voicing your opinion!

Or hit me up on Twitter or LinkedIn if you want to chat.

[^1]SSD Benchmarks

[^2]Nyquist-Shannon Sampling Theorem

[^3][Quantization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantization_(signal_processing)

[^4]Chroma Subsampling

item.title: Grace Blackwell needs a new scheduler: 27% more usable GPUs from the same racks (132 pts)
item.description:
