Not all high-speed interconnects are created equal, and using the wrong one can be quite costly: running the same distributed training job over InfiniBand rather than NVLink can degrade performance by 43%.

Historically, NVLink was limited to communication within a single node, meaning that multi-node AI workloads were forced to communicate over InfiniBand or a cloud equivalent (EFA on AWS, GPUDirect-TCPX on GCP). NVIDIA’s NVL72 systems remove this limitation by connecting all 72 GPUs in a rack with a unified NVLink fabric, so GPUs on different nodes can exchange data with an order of magnitude more bandwidth.

However, maximizing the benefits of NVL72 systems is highly dependent on workload placement: a multi-node job spread across racks is still bottlenecked by InfiniBand. Preserving rack-locality gets harder as hardware failures take nodes offline and jobs finishing at different times scatter free capacity across racks.

This blog covers the communication bottleneck in large-scale training and inference, the NVL72 rack-scale fabric, and slice sizing for resilience to GPU failures, as well as how the SkyPilot Platform keeps multi-node jobs rack-local through topology-aware placement, in-place recovery from hardware failures, and automatic defragmentation of shared clusters.

Frontier training jobs run across thousands of GPUs. Doing so requires answering two questions:

  1. How do you shard your model across GPUs to ensure that it can actually run?
  2. Given your compute budget, how many copies of the sharded model can you run to maximize training throughput?

The first question is typically answered with a combination of:

  • Tensor Parallelism (TP): splitting a layer’s weight matrices across GPUs
  • Expert Parallelism (EP): placing a mixture-of-experts (MoE) layer’s experts on different GPUs
  • Pipeline Parallelism (PP): splitting a model layer-wise across GPUs

The answer to the second question sets the degree of Data Parallelism (DP): the number of copies of the sharded model that train in parallel, each on a different slice of the training data.

Of these parallelism strategies, tensor parallelism’s all-reduce and expert parallelism’s all-to-all communication patterns sit on the critical path during training, making them the most important to keep on NVLink (§9.1.2).

Tensor Parallelism

Tensor parallelism splits the weight matrices inside each layer across GPUs, so every GPU only stores and computes a slice of each layer.

Transformer layers are made up of two blocks: self-attention and a multi-layer perceptron (MLP). At its core, each block is two matrix multiplications (GEMMs) in a row. Megatron-LM (§3) showed that by partitioning a block’s first GEMM column-wise and its second GEMM row-wise, the GPUs only need to synchronize via all-reduce once per block, after the second GEMM, instead of after each one.

Even with this optimization, tensor parallelism still requires two all-reduces per transformer layer during the forward pass. These all-reduce steps sit on the critical path during training because they cannot be fully overlapped with computation. As a result, tensor parallelism is typically kept on NVLink: Hugging Face measured a 43% drop in training throughput when it moved off NVLink onto InfiniBand.

Expert Parallelism

In a mixture-of-experts (MoE) layer, the MLP block is replaced by many smaller MLPs, called experts, and a router that sends each token to a small subset of experts. Expert parallelism splits MoE layers such that these small, independent experts are placed on different GPUs.

Under expert parallelism, each MoE layer requires two all-to-all communication steps during the forward pass, dispatch and combine. A router selects the top-k experts for each token and dispatches tokens to the GPUs that have those experts in memory. Each GPU then computes its local experts on the tokens it received via a single grouped matrix multiplication. Finally, the expert outputs are sent back to each token's original GPU and combined.

As models add more MoE layers and route each token to more experts, the volume of all-to-all traffic grows, introducing a communication bottleneck.

Training an MoE model with 64-way expert parallelism spreads each MoE layer’s experts across 64 GPUs. On standard 8-GPU servers, that moves the all-to-all traffic off high-bandwidth NVLink and through much narrower InfiniBand interconnects where unoptimized communication can consume up to 60% of training time (§1.2). On NVL72 systems, all 64 GPUs stay within a single NVLink domain, effectively eliminating the communication bottleneck (§9.2.2).

The parallelism techniques discussed above are not unique to training. Beyond enabling inference engines to serve models that are too large for a single GPU, model parallelism can also improve throughput. Splitting a model's weights across more GPUs frees up memory for the KV cache, so the engine can process more concurrent requests or support larger context windows. In some cases, the freed memory grows faster than the number of GPUs: in one vLLM benchmark, splitting a model tensor-parallel across two GPUs increased the amount of KV cache blocks by 13.9x and delivered 3.9x more throughput.

Expert parallelism follows the same logic. With a low degree of expert parallelism, each GPU holds many experts, leaving less room for the KV cache. WideEP, which refers to expert-parallel configurations spanning multiple nodes, significantly reduces the number of experts per GPU. The trade-off is network traffic: every all-to-all now spans more GPUs. On standard 8-GPU servers, an expert-parallel group can span at most eight GPUs before it has to communicate over InfiniBand, where per-GPU bandwidth drops 18x. NVL72 removes this limit by keeping all 72 GPUs in a rack on NVLink. When serving DeepSeek-R1 at interactive speeds, GB200 NVL72 with 32-way expert parallelism delivers up to 4.4x higher throughput per GPU than 8-GPU B200 servers, which are capped at 8-way.

NVL72 extends NVLink from a single node to the entire rack, so the whole rack acts like a gigantic accelerator with shared memory.

Every GPU on the NVL72 rack has 18 NVLink ports each delivering 100 GB/s of bidirectional bandwidth, which sums up to a total of 1.8 TB/s for each GPU. Each NVLink port on a given GPU maps to one of 18 NVSwitch chips that power the rack's fabric backplane. Because each NVSwitch chip accepts 72 NVLink lines, one from each of the GPUs, the aggregate internal bandwidth within the rack is 130 TB/s.

This network topology ensures that the fabric is fully non-blocking, meaning that any GPU in the rack can transmit data to any other GPU with uniform latency, making it ideal for large-scale distributed AI workloads.

With NVL72 systems, it is tempting to allocate entire 18-node racks to workloads to maximize cluster utilization. In practice, teams actually get more usable capacity out of their cluster by leaving a couple of spare nodes in each rack.

GPUs are unreliable. On its gigawatt-scale supercluster, Meta measured a mean time between interruptions (MTBI) of roughly 490 days per 4-GPU node after putting significant engineering effort into improving reliability. NVL72 clusters make the 72-GPU rack the atomic unit of compute, which increases the fault blast radius by 18x compared to the 4-GPU nodes that make up the rack. The MTBI for the rack is given by:

Based on the formula above, a rack would be interrupted roughly every 490 / 18 ≈ 27 days. If jobs are allocated entire 18-node racks, each of those interruptions makes the entire rack unschedulable until the failed node is repaired. On a 128-rack cluster, this means that a rack would become unusable for full-rack jobs roughly every 5 hours.

Reserving two nodes per rack as spares changes this. When a node fails, a spare in the same rack replaces it, so a single node failure no longer takes the entire rack out of commission. The cost is that two nodes per rack sit idle while everything is healthy.

To quantify this trade-off, NVIDIA modeled how different slice sizes affect usable capacity on a 128-rack (2,304-node) cluster as the share of unavailable nodes grows.

At SkyPilot, we manage tens of thousands of our customers’ GPUs, and on production NVL72 clusters we have measured unavailability rates of around 2%. At that rate, NVIDIA’s model shows that 16-node slices provide 27% more usable capacity than 18-node slices (2,037 vs. 1,602 nodes). They also beat 9-node slices by 4%, even though two 9-node slices fill a rack exactly: with 9-node slices, every failure costs half a rack, while with 16-node slices, the first two failures in a rack are fully absorbed. Compared with 8-node slices, 16-node slices give each job twice as many GPUs per NVLink domain while giving up less than 1% of usable capacity until node unavailability exceeds about 3.3%.

Sixteen nodes is also a natural size for distributed AI workloads: 64 GPUs is a power of two, which matches how parallelism groups are typically sized.

So far, we have covered why the most communication-heavy parallelism techniques belong on NVLink, how NVL72 extends NVLink from a single node to the whole rack, and why 16-node slices with two spare nodes per rack get the most usable capacity out of production clusters. SkyPilot puts this into practice by placing each slice on a single rack, recovering from hardware failures in-place, and keeping whole racks free as jobs come and go.

Schedulers need to understand the hardware

Choosing the right slice size is only the first step. How do researchers ensure that each slice of a multi-node training run actually lands on a single rack?

Naive schedulers split multi-node jobs across racks, forcing workers to communicate over InfiniBand (400 Gb/s per direction) instead of NVLink (1.8 TB/s bidirectional):

SkyPilot’s Topology-Aware Scheduler (TAS) ensures that workers are colocated on the same rack:

For multi-rack workloads, TAS splits the job into 16-node (configurable) slices, and places them each on their own rack with two spare nodes. Then, when SkyPilot’s GPU Manager detects GPU failures, SkyPilot Frontier Trainer can hot swap the faulty node with one of the reserved healthy nodes while the remaining nodes continue running without interruption. If there are no remaining spares in the same rack, Frontier Trainer will reschedule the slice on the faulty rack to a healthy rack:

To quantify the impact of slice-based scheduling, NVIDIA’s GR00T team compared the effect of two different scheduling policies during pre-training of GR00T N1.7, a multimodal foundation model for humanoid robots, on 512 GB300 GPUs across 128 nodes. The first run used a naive scheduler that placed nodes across an arbitrary number of racks. The second run was scheduled with a rack-aware, slice-based policy like the one in Figure 10, which placed it on exactly 8 racks. Rack-aware placement raised throughput by 14.4%, cutting each iteration from 1.59 s to 1.39 s.

On a 10,000-GPU cluster, the same speedup saves roughly $16.7K per training hour. That’s about $400K saved for every training day, just by making better scheduling decisions.

Fragmentation blocks rack-scale jobs

So far we have explored how topology-aware scheduling works in isolation. In practice, large clusters are typically shared: heterogeneous workloads such as pre-training runs, RL rollouts, and batch inference all compete for the same resources. TAS bin packs workloads within the same rack at scheduling time, but jobs finish at different times, leaving free nodes scattered across racks. This is fragmentation: the cluster has enough free GPUs to run a rack-scale job, but because they’re spread across racks, the job can’t be scheduled.

SkyPilot’s Automatic Defragmentation (Auto Defrag) is built to address this. When a job is blocked by topology rather than capacity, Auto Defrag finds the least disruptive set of workloads to preempt to free up an entire rack. Those workloads are rescheduled on other racks, allowing the blocked job to be scheduled.

Auto Defrag only preempts workloads that restart safely, such as managed jobs that resume from a checkpoint. Interactive development environments are left alone unless an admin explicitly opts them in.

Large-scale AI workloads are distributed by default, and their most network-intensive communication patterns sit on the critical path. Rack-scale systems like NVL72 aim to address this bottleneck in hardware, but the hardware alone doesn't guarantee the speedup. These systems require rack-aware placement, resilience to hardware failures, and dynamic rebalancing as jobs come and go. The SkyPilot Platform is purpose-built to close that gap: Topology-Aware Scheduling keeps multi-node jobs on NVLink, Frontier Trainer swaps in a healthy spare when GPU Manager detects hardware failures, and Automatic Defragmentation keeps shared racks open for large jobs. If you're wrangling NVL72 clusters, we'd love to chat.

item.title: Zombie stats: Where the numbers AI quotes come from (148 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://trakkr.ai/trakkr-research/zombie-stats, See on Hacker News

Following one number back to its source

We asked ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude and Google’s AI Overviews 200 questions that call for a number, the kind people ask every day. Then we clicked the citations, and kept clicking. Here is one trail, from the answer to the end.

Google AI Overviews

What percentage of salespeople give up after one follow-up?

44% of salespeople give up after just one follow-up attempt.

  • 44%
  • 44%
  • 44%
  • 44%
  • 44%
A sales firm’s stats page2020

44% of salespeople give up after one follow-up attempt (source).

A freelance writer’s sample articleby 2017

80 Percent of Sales Require 5 Follow-up Calls after Meeting; 44 Percent Salespeople Give Up After One Follow-up

No study behind itThis page cites no research.

  1. In the answer

    Every assistant got the same question: “What percentage of salespeople give up after one follow-up?” All five assistants gave the same figure, and only ChatGPT said the evidence behind it was unclear.

  2. One click in

    Google AI Overviews cited a sales firm’s stats page, from 2020. The number is right there. Its “source” link goes to a writing sample.

  3. Two clicks in

    That leads to a freelance writer’s sample article, online by 2017. The number is in its headline. It lists two slide decks, a blog list and two news stories. None is a study of follow-ups.

  4. The end of the trail

    That’s where the trail ends. We tried every other route to this number we could find, and each one stopped at a page that cites no research. This is what we mean by a zombie stat: a number that keeps getting repeated with no study behind it.

Most numbers aren’t like this one. The trouble is that you can’t tell which ones are from the answer. This one came with the same confident tone and the same kind of citation as any other, and all five assistants agreed on it. So we followed 1,285 statistics the same way.

Fewer than half lead back to a study

We took a random sample of the statistics each assistant cited, 1,285 in all, and walked every trail the same way: the cited page, then that page’s source, up to five pages deep. Where a page named a source without a link, we searched for it.

40% reached a study that says the same thing. Another 8% reached the study, but the number or its context had changed on the way. The rest never got there: 40% stopped at a source we couldn’t check, because it was locked, gone or silent on the number, and 11% led nowhere at all.

ChatGPT did best, and quoted the fewest numbers: 1.3 per answer, against 6.8 for Claude. The other four landed between 38% and 46%, too close to rank.

To check this wasn’t down to the questions we picked, we also traced 300 statistics from Google AI Overviews answers to real everyday searches. 40% were sourced, about the same share.

AI mostly cites pages that repeat the number

The AI mostly wasn’t making numbers up. The page it cited had the figure 82% of the time. But only 21% of the pages cited for a number were the original research.

More than half were company blogs. Add news stories and statistics roundups and you have most of the citations: pages that repeat figures from somewhere else, often without linking to it.

The first page made a big difference. When a trail started at a research firm or a government page, it reached a matching study 61% of the time. From a company blog, 37%; from a statistics roundup, 35%. Even research firms fell short 38% of the time, often because the full report sat behind a form.

A citation tells you where the AI found a number, not where the number came from.

Some numbers change along the way

Reaching the study didn’t always mean the number held. Of the statistics that got there, 17% had changed on the way. The digits moved only about one time in four. Usually it was the context: what was measured, the year, the source, or who was asked.

What changed, across every change we logged

The number changed
26%

What was measured changed
20%

The year changed
17%

The source changed
16%

Who was asked changed
14%

The place changed
4%

In one case, a 2004 study of 15 women judging health websites turned into a claim about first impressions of every website. Below are the clearest trails we followed, each checked by hand.

The zombie stats

Ask five assistants the same question and you’ll often get five different numbers. On 28 of the 71 questions where all five gave a percentage, we got four or five different figures.

Across those questions, the typical gap between the highest figure and the lowest was 16 points.

When all five agreed, the number wasn’t any more likely to check out. They gave the same figure on 10 questions, and of the 5 we traced, 2 were sourced. The statistics quoted by three or more assistants did no better: 11 of 29 were sourced.

Four were quoted by all five assistants, and we couldn’t find a study behind any of them.

What to do with a statistic from an AI

Treat it as a lead rather than a source. Here’s what we’d do, whether you use these numbers or publish them.

If you use them

  1. Follow the citation, then follow it again.

    If the cited page is a list of statistics or a company blog, use its own link to go one page further. Keep going until you reach the study itself, or until you can’t.

  2. Check who was asked, how many, and when.

    Most of the changes we found were in the context, not the digits: one country’s poll, a ten-year-old study, fifteen people.

  3. Don’t take agreement as a check.

    Five assistants giving the same number isn’t five sources. The numbers they repeated most were no better sourced than the rest.

If you publish them

  1. Put the method next to the number.

    The sample, the date and a link to the source, on the same page as the figure, so the next page, and the next answer, can trace it back to you.

  2. Keep the findings in the open.

    Reports behind a form were a common dead end: even trails that started at a research firm fell short 38% of the time. Put the headline numbers and the method on an open page.

  3. See which page AI cites for your numbers.

    It is often a roundup or a blog that copied you, sometimes with an older figure. That page decides what people hear.

item.description:
URL: https://martinfowler.com/bliki/LLM-Voice.html, See on Hacker News

Sometimes when I read a post, I get the growing feeling that I'm reading the output of an LLM. I can't necessarily define why, although there are the common tells (it's not the em-dashes, it's the load-bearing tapestries). As I do this my desire to read on atrophies, sometimes to the point of revulsion

There are tools out there that claim to be able to tell the difference between LLM-written prose and the old-fashioned biological product. I'm wary of them, partly due skeptism about their accuracy, but also because it rather misses the point. The reaction to LLM-Voice is a human one, that sense that we are in an uncanny valley of prose. By the time I'd reach for a tool to tell me what I'm reading, it's already too late, even if it confidently tells me there's no LLM present.

I'm also suspicious of my own ability to accurately recognize LLM voice. Language changes over time, so a common sign of age is complaining about the language of the youngs. I'm inclined to bristle at prose that talks about “adopting a new sales motion,” or “a sharp round-up of news”. But I've heard these constructs coming out of human mouths, so that's more a generational difference rather than between carbon and silicon. (And as a transplanted Brit, don't get me started on Americanisms, I'm sure I'll get used to them momentarily.)

Right now I urge authors to be extra-wary of LLM-Voice. In particular I strongly recommend that authors should not fall into the trap of getting the LLM to write a draft. Even if it's edited by a human, it's very hard to expel the LLM-Voice - thus causing the uncanny valley reaction. 1 Even accepting suggestions of rephrasing is dangerous. I have heard of people using LLMs to develop outline and structure, that may be ok, but only as far as an outline. 2 Authors should fill the prose themselves.

1: Very hard, but not impossible. I've come across one case where I do know the first draft was entirely done by LLM, but I detected no LLM Voice when I read the final piece. It did, however, need a professional editor at a major periodical publication to clean it up.

2: My policy on this site, is that anyone who uses AI to help them write should declare how they used it, usually in the acknowledgments. This is partly for transparency, and partly so that readers can learn useful ways to use AI. In my own case, I don't use AI for generating prose, nor for help in structure. The only way I use it for writing is as a search tool (but I verify any information by going to the source).

Say Your Writing is even more important in the age of LLMs. I habitually speak the words in my head and then write them down (and then edit what I've just written). This advice is particularly important to anyone who has any desire to communicate regularly with writing. Like many things, learning to be a good writer relies on lots of practice. It's a skill worth the time to acquire, but surrendering to an LLM will undermine any progress.

In time it may be that LLMs will be so good that we can't tell the difference. In many ways, that's more worrying. Like most writers, I find writing an almost-essential tool for thinking. Often it's only by writing something down, that I can really get my thoughts on a topic into coherence. I've often started an essay knowing I don't really understand something, but the act of wrestling with the words forces me to overcome my confusions. As more people delegate writing to LLMs they will also delegate thinking and comprehension to LLMs. I don't want to do that, where's the fun of writing then?

Although avoiding LLM-Voice is a general rule, it isn't an absolute one. An important example is that of Jim Highsmith (who contributes to this site). He finds working with an LLM is essential to his writing to overcome the bane of Parkinson's disease. I'll gladly deal with LLM-Voice in order to continue imbibing my old friend's wisdom.

A more awkward case is that of translation. Many of my colleagues aren't comfortable in English, it is their second or fourth language. Some have found LLM translation an important part to their communication with those of us who know rather less Marathi. But I also would prefer rather a genuine human's clunky prose to the smooth but soulless LLM.

There are situations where it would be reasonable for even a native Englishman to let LLMs write the prose. Such as if I'm writing a form letter to an official, or preparing a report I suspect no-one will ever read 3. Maybe most documentation in the future will only be read by LLMs, and they won't have my uncanny valley worries. But if I want to communicate with humans, my humanity has to shine (or at least ooze) out of my prose.

3: Michael Nygard commented: “There you really aren't trying to communicate thoughts from one person to other people. You're communicating with a process rather than a human. A human may open the envelope but that person is acting as a component in a cybernetic organism.”

Acknowledgements

Alessio Ferri, Caer Sanders, Ian Cartwright, Jie Jessie Xia, Joshua Kerievsky, Michael Feathers, Michael Nygard, Scott Davies, and Wei Zhang commented on drafts of this post.

I did not use AI or LLMs in any way while writing this post.

The investigation is expected to be complete at some point next year.

The Oulu Police Department has opened a preliminary investigation into the activities at Google's data centre construction site in Muhos, following a request from the Finnish Supervisory Agency to look into the matter.

The department has received five requests for an investigation related to the Muhos site, all of which will be addressed in the preliminary probe.

The data centre construction work is part of the tech giant's 13 billion euro investment in Finland.

Police said the matter is being investigated under the criminal heading of suspected environmental damage. They noted that other possible charges may be clarified as the preliminary investigation proceeds.

Police said that, based on current information, there have been irregularities and shortcomings in drainage and water management at the data centre project's worksite, which is run by Google's local subsidiary Tuike Finland.

The preliminary investigation is expected to take a good deal of time, police said, adding that efforts will be made to complete the probe during 2027.

The department said that it will aim to provide more information about the matter in December.

Authority's request

In a press release issued last week, the Finnish Supervisory Agency explained that it ordered Tuike Finland to halt construction work on two data centre projects — in Muhos and Kajaani-Otanmäki — because required environmental impact assessments for both projects remained incomplete.

The company complied, confirming on 14 October that preparatory work had been suspended at both sites.

Among other issues, the authority found Tuike Finland's water management plans insufficient to prove that water-related environmental impacts can be properly controlled.

It said the firm needs to submit a detailed water management plan by 5 November, including planned structures, timelines and independent water monitoring, accounting for heavy rainfall, snowmelt, and risks from acidic black shale soils in the area.

The authority noted that if adequate action is not taken, it may pursue formal enforcement measures, including a conditional fine.

item.title: Manifestos, Fear, and 'Loser Thinking': Inside Proton's AI Reckoning (141 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.404media.co/manifestos-fear-and-loser-thinking-inside-protons-ai-reckoning/, See on Hacker News

Andy Yen, the CEO of Proton, had a message for an employee in the company’s security Slack channel who urged the company to at least take a few days to pentest newly written code before pushing it live. “That’s bullshit and loser thinking. Of course it’s possible to be fast and secure,” Yen wrote in the channel at the end of August. “Stop thinking always of how to be slower, and focus more on how to be faster.”

In a follow-up message, Yen reiterated his point: “only losers think like that.” His ultimate message for the team was to “stop lovingly handcrafting all our code and use AI more.”

That exchange was just one of many that showed how Yen and other company executives are aggressively pushing Proton towards AI. Proton is a Swiss company that famously makes the encrypted email service Proton Mail and a suite of privacy and security-focused products, including an encrypted drive service, an authenticator app, a password manager, and more.

In the last few months, Yen set up an email address for employees to contact if they come across anything blocking adoption of AI at Proton, so leadership can “ruthlessly smash everything that stands in the way of AI velocity;” Proton installed software on workers’ computers that track how much AI code the company is generating; and Yen said this is the last year that Proton will hire engineers at all, and instead only hire people to build things with AI.

That AI push came to head this week when 404 Media reported Proton said it would re-interview staff about their use of AI, with the clear implication that those interviews, and employees’ willingness to embrace AI, could decide whether a worker is fired or not.

404 Media spoke to eight current and one former Proton employees and reviewed Slack chats, meeting recordings, and an AI manifesto written by the company’s CTO. Our reporting reveals a culture of fear inside Proton, where many employees are hesitant to even mildly critique Yen’s views or discuss engineering problems. Workers describe an environment where employees have genuine concerns about security or being asked to develop security products with AI, but feel unable to voice them, lest Yen berates them in front of everyone or threatens their employment at the company.

“The CEO is in full AI psychosis and has been for a while now,” one of the sources told 404 Media.

Our reporting also paints a picture of Proton that is likely very different to the public’s perception of a company with a goal of carefully protecting privacy: one that in reality is barreling ahead with AI as quickly as possible so it can achieve the explicit goal of more annual revenue.

“Due to insufficient velocity,” Proton is not on track to achieve its annual recurring revenue target by the end of the year, one internal document obtained by 404 Media reads. Proton’s year-over-year growth is also “far away from what the market today considers to be good,” and, “By all metrics that matter, we’re an underperforming company.”

In response to detailed questions from 404 Media, a Proton spokesperson did not dispute any of our reporting or characterization of what’s happening inside of the company. 

“It’s clear that some people at Proton are unhappy with our direction, or misunderstand it, and many people are anxious,” they said. “In our determination to move fast, we have sometimes been too blunt or too slow in explaining ourselves to our people. We will work on that, as their questions are the ones we most need to answer.”

💡

Do you know anything else about Proton? I would love to hear from you. Using a non-work device, you can message me securely on Signal at joseph.404 or send me an email at joseph@404media.co.

Yen, a former CERN particle physicist, projects a measured approach in public, but internally he acts more like what one employee described as a “petulant child.” In May, Proton announced it was implementing post-quantum cryptography which should protect against future attacks from quantum computers. The work took years of effort, with one caveat that it would not work on older emails, only those written after the feature’s launch, at least for the moment. Yen was not happy that Proton was drawing attention to this limitation.

In a Slack channel dedicated to thanking people for their work, Yen jumped in. “Get it fixed,” he wrote, referring to Proton’s Reddit post announcing the feature. “Now Reddit is pissed and we look worse than Tuta,” he added, referring to a Proton competitor. When employees explained to Yen the nuances of the encryption and why that was not immediately possible, Yen wrote, “I find this whole thing stupid. You cannot announce this in this way.”

“Now we are left with two shitty choices. Deprioritize more important tasks for the business to re-encrypt old emails, or constantly get attacked online for not doing it. So maybe you can enlighten me on which of the two shitty choices we will take,” he wrote. “In the future there are two options. Either you guys are confident enough to not fuck this up, or you get my advice to make sure it is not fucked up,” he added. He then told a member of the team that made it to “go on Reddit.”

“So go on there with your personal account and comment to set the record straight,” he wrote. “Perception is more important than truth, the truth doesn’t matter if you don’t win on perception.”

One employee told 404 Media, “Whatever persona Andy [Yen] has out of Proton, he’s a straight up bully inside. He routinely breaks his little facade in Slack and calls people losers and stupid, often for stuff he’s paying them for.”

Ever since launching Proton Mail in 2014 after the Snowden revelations, Proton has steadily introduced new products that make Proton more of a worksuite than a simple email provider. More recently, those products were focused around AI, with the launch of Lumo, a large language model (LLM) chatbot that the company says doesn’t log conversations or train on user data. In June, Proton launched a 2.0 version of its chatbot.

Up until this point, Yen’s public comments on AI were relatively tame. In an August interview with WIRED, he said Proton is “building AI features and AI tools, because I think if the privacy companies do not find a way to step in to build privacy-first AI, we are essentially ceding the future to tech companies that don’t have the best interests of users at heart,” and that the company was “capitalizing” on the backlash to corporatized, invasive AI from companies like Google. Last year, Yen and Proton were criticized for statements he made suggesting the Republican Party and Donald Trump would be harder on Big Tech than Democrats. 

Toward the end of August, Yen’s internal tone on AI shifted to having Proton use it as much as possible, and as quickly as possible, according to the Slack chats and multiple employees.

“The train is coming, get onboard or get crushed. Don’t be the professional fax machine operator in the internet age,” he wrote to the security Slack channel. “I think by the end of this year most developers stop programming and start writing specs for tests that AI will code and run, to validate AI written code that humans will no longer be able to review. This will be the last year that we hire engineers, and starting next year we hire what we used to call product managers, to build things with AI.”

AI is changing how cybersecurity works, with AI agents hacking into companies, and AI assisting in the discovery of gaping vulnerabilities in important code. Many companies across the privacy and security space are grappling with how to deal with AI, either in the development of their products or how to defend themselves against hackers who are using AI. Some may do this carefully. Others are trying to do it as quickly as possible for profit. This account of Proton’s own reckoning with AI provides an unprecedented insight into what is happening inside one security-focused company users especially trust. 

Initially, using AI was banned inside Proton, but the company has since approved AI for all sorts of use cases internally, including processing financial data, drafting customer-facing responses on Reddit and LinkedIn, and writing code “except when that source code contains information that would give immediate advantage to a competitor” or is related to “innovation or R&D [research and development],” according to an internal Proton document seen by 404 Media. Ninety percent of code at Proton in October was written by AI, the company’s CTO Bart Butler said in a meeting, according to audio 404 Media obtained. Much of that code is written with Anthropic’s Claude, multiple employees told 404 Media. And Yen tells employees in Slack chats to use Claude, too. 

“We are a tech company against Big Tech who are spending loads on Claude,” one employee told 404 Media.

In the “bullshit and loser thinking” conversation, another employee pushed Yen for specifics on ensuring that AI-generated code was free of security issues. “AI won’t magically solve our problems, because security is low in our prioritization at present,” the engineer said. Yen didn’t respond directly, and went on to insult one of the other employees in front of the entire channel. The employee “is saying his usual bs of we can do it but we will be even slower than we are today and I’m saying only losers think like that,” Yen wrote, adding that workers should prompt “better.”

“You have the models and the time every developer should be doing this and checking their code which they were doing before manually but now they can do faster with AI,” Yen added. (One employee stressed that engineers still strive to build in a secure way.) 

The second clear signal that Proton was going deep into AI for many employees happened when Butler, the CTO, published a self-described AI manifesto one Friday afternoon last month.

“Your old job is gone,” the manifesto, posted to Slack, told engineers. It laid out a future for Proton that fully embraced AI, and said if the company did not do so, that posed an “existential threat to the success of the mission itself.”

Butler said that Proton needs to change in three key ways: accept that an engineers’ job is now to help LLMs write better code, faster; that Proton needs to get to the point where most code is not reviewed by humans but by AI; and to more fundamentally change the company as a whole, and “commit, as an organization, to the transformation that the moment requires.”

One Proton employee replied in Slack, “Perhaps scaring people with: We are in a new world. ‘Programming’ is dead [...] your old job is gone wasn’t really necessary on a Friday afternoon.”

Butler replied, “It’s supposed to be provocative, because it needs to be. I suggest you read it, think about it over the weekend, and come with your questions to me on Monday rather than on Slack. Thanks!”

An employee told 404 Media, “​​People were surprised and somewhat cringed out, since the document clearly exaggerates what you can do with LLMs today and doesn't address any of the problems you get in return for giving up your code base to the AI Jesus (e.g. AI cannot really maintain a large code base over time).” Another called it “ethically bankrupt.”

Earlier this week, Proton sent the email to employees saying they would re-interview workers about how they use AI in their jobs. The tone was clear; you may lose your job because of these interviews, current employees told 404 Media. “These re-interviews are consequential,” the email read. Soon after, a senior employee spoke up in Slack to Yen about the re-interviewing process. He suggested instead that Proton detect who is falling behind and support them and enforce high quality training.

Yen’s response was blunt: “Let’s put it this way, we already know more or less who is behind. If we were giving up on them, we would not bother with this process.”

The employee replied, “That messaging is fear-based. Which is probably why I suspect there are dozens of other employees watching us talk about this live and except for [other employee] no one else is chiming in.”

“People shouldn’t be scared to talk about this in public and to push back on you and leadership. A fear based culture feels like a cancer to me. It’s the opposite of engineering, you need to talk about things, even uncomfortable things,” they added. Yen eventually told the employee, in front of everyone: “If you are making the accusation that this is a financially driven decision and you don’t trust me when I tell you it’s not, then I think this might not be the place for you.”

Only one other employee chimed in during that exchange: “It’s about the culture you instil, people don’t want to feel like they’re on a tightrope, and yes we understand you want to move fast but there needs to be a balance, people also need support, not everyone is the same.”

“It was also faster for my parents to beat me until I ate my vegetables but I’m not sure it was healthy,” they added.

The exchange with Yen was unusual not only in that someone was debating some of Yen’s ideas, but also that it directly referenced the culture of fear at Proton. “Whenever someone talks back to Andy it tends to be highlighted since very few people talk back to him,” one employee told 404 Media.

Mistral released Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk), a 1-trillion-parameter multimodal model, now available with improved coding, cybersecurity, and reasoning efficiency. It leads open-weight benchmarks in coding and defensive security while offering three reasoning modes for cost-performance balance. Fully open-weight and European-trained, it empowers sovereign AI with customizable, self-hosted deployment options.

We release the weights of Le Chonk, advancing the frontier of open models in agentic coding and cybersecurity.

Earlier this month, we released Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk), our flagship 1-trillion-parameter, natively multimodal model, in public preview. The response to the preview has exceeded our expectations, and we're grateful to our developer community, early-access customers, and partners for their support, collaboration, and feedback.

Since then, we've put that feedback to work while continuing to scale reinforcement learning, driving massive improvements in coding and defensive cybersecurity. Gains continue to accelerate, with no signs of saturation.

Today, we're releasing the weights of this improved Mistral Large 4. The new model also features substantial gains in reasoning efficiency that give developers greater performance while lowering inference costs.

Mistral Large 4 ranks as the best open-weight model for coding and among the world's most capable open models overall. Trained from scratch on European infrastructure with clear lineage from inception to release, it gives organizations a trusted foundation for Sovereign AI

Mistral is defining the sovereign AI category and leading the open frontier. We're committed to building the world's most capable models and releasing them openly, giving developers, enterprises, and institutions the power to own, customize, and control their AI.

Built for the Builders.

Mistral Large 4 entered public preview with strong results across leading coding benchmarks. Just three weeks of additional reinforcement learning have since propelled it to the forefront of open-weight coding, taking the lead on FrontierCode and Terminal-Bench while matching the best open-weight models on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index with substantially greater token efficiency.

On Cognition's private FrontierCode 2.0 benchmark, which assesses end-to-end code quality and whether a repository maintainer would merge the agent's change, Mistral Large 4 leads with a score of 19.7%.

Pushing the pareto frontier for agentic coding.

Mistral Large 4 delivers frontier coding performance with significantly fewer tokens, making sophisticated coding agents more economical to run at scale.

On the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, Mistral Large 4 scores 48%, effectively tied with the leading open-weight model, GLM-5.3, while using 47% fewer tokens per task on average.

The gains extend to terminal-based coding workflows. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, Mistral Large 4 improved by 13 percentage points to 41% compared to its public preview, taking the lead among open-weight models while reducing output tokens by 30%.

To give developers greater control over this tradeoff between performance and cost, Mistral Large 4 now supports three reasoning modes:

Mode

Recommended Use

Low

Simple tasks; replaces ‘None’ reasoning mode

Medium

Everyday tasks

High (default)

Hardest use cases requiring high precision and thorough reasoning

Beyond benchmarks, Mistral Large 4's coding capabilities are validated by human preference. In Surge Code's blind pairwise evaluations, Mistral Large 4 was preferred over leading open-weight models including GLM-5.3, Kimi K3, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, ranking behind only Claude Opus 5.5 among the models evaluated.

Built for the Defenders. 

Since its preview, we've been working with leading cybersecurity vendors to evaluate Mistral Large 4 in real-world environments to test Mistral Large 4’s strengths in vulnerability reproduction and patching.

Mistral Large 4 scores 51% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index, which measures a model’s ability to discover vulnerabilities in a codebase, reproduce and validate them, and patch them without breaking existing functionality. Crucially, Mistral Large 4 handles these legitimate defensive security tasks without unnecessary refusals.

Safety has improved alongside capability. Our model’s built-in guardrails distinguishes between defensive and malicious, offensive cybersecurity tasks. It retains strong performance on Cyber benchmarks, while achieving an average refusal rate of 96.6% on malicious cyber requests, the highest we measure among open models.

Here’s what global leaders in cybersecurity have to say about Mistral Large 4:

In the time since the preview, we carefully monitored cybersecurity-related use in our live traffic. Though we observed the model refusing to comply with black-box attacks against live targets, we see a potential for uplift to conduct real attacks. We are modifying our guardrails accordingly, and will continue updating them in the months to come. 

We are also providing enterprise design partners such as Orange Cyberdefense, with preview access to a specialized variant of Mistral Large 4 optimized for advanced cybersecurity workflows, including penetration testing, vulnerability assessment, and red-teaming. Access is subject to rigorous vetting and contractual safeguards, with testing restricted to owned or explicitly authorized systems in controlled environments.

Meanwhile, customers are tailoring Mistral Large 4 with proprietary security data, policies, detection logic, and threat environments using Mistral Forge. For well-defined cybersecurity tasks, it can be further optimized into smaller, task-specific variants for greater accuracy, making security applications more effective.

Learn more about sovereign AI for cybersecurity and how to work with us.

Built for Work.

Mistral Large 4 has continued improving on a range of broad enterprise-use metrics. 


For finance-related work, we improved the model’s ability to perform real-world workflows, especially ones involving the creation and editing of spreadsheets for finance and accounting use cases. This is reflected in our Finch scores climbing to 73.3%, second only to Kimi K3 for open models.

Web browsing is a critical part of a majority of knowledge work. Our RL pipeline enabled us to reach 84.5% on BrowseComp (starting from an SFT checkpoint that was achieving 75%). This brings Mistral Large 4 at a higher performance than models like GLM-5.3 or DeepSeek Flash 4.1 1017.

Agents deployed by an organization need to be secure. Whether deployed to internal members or external users, agents shouldn’t open you up to threats like system prompt exfiltration or malicious code injection. RL increased our gains on the B3 Agent Security Benchmark, with Mistral Large 4 resisting 97.1% of attacks vs 93.3% in Preview. This places it at the top of the OSS frontier, meaning anyone hosting the model can run a safe agent without additional tuning.

This major investment by Mistral AI reinforces the choice La Banque Postale made over a year ago and underscores the relevance of the long-term strategic partnership we are building together: supporting the emergence of an open and sovereign European AI leader. For a public and citizen bank, technological sovereignty is not optional; it is a key prerequisite for maintaining our customers' trust. The introduction of this open model unlocks new opportunities and use cases. By partnering with Mistral AI, our ambition is to combine the best of human expertise and digital technology to deliver an enhanced experience of both customers and employees over the long term.

Zakaria Moursli, Executive Vice President, Operational Performance, Payments and Digital Services, La Banque Postale

See it in Action

Cyber Vulnerability Triage: an agent reads incoming vulnerability reports, investigates the source code and product context, reproduces the flaws in an isolated sandbox, then writes and iterates on a patch until a canary exploit no longer works.

Agentic webdev: with no human help, Mistral Large 4 builds Orbital Trace, a live 3D map of roughly 19,000 satellites and debris pieces orbiting Earth. It pulls real tracking data, writes the app, uses it in a browser to catch its own bugs and slowdowns, then fixes what an independent reviewer flags until all requirements pass.

Quantum chemistry solver: Mistral Large 4 writes, from scratch, software that calculates where electrons sit in a molecule, and checks its answers against a standard chemistry tool. It then builds a 3D page around it: pick a molecule such as benzene or water, drag a slider to pull it apart, and watch the electrons regroup as the bond breaks.

Built for Sovereignty.

As organizations build AI around their knowledge and workflows, sovereignty means that they retain control of the models they depend on and the intelligence they create. 

With Mistral Large 4, that control begins with the model itself. Organizations have the ability to inspect, customize, and deploy the model on their own infrastructure. They can use and improve Mistral Large 4 without depending on Mistral to serve it through an API. Mistral Large 4 was developed and trained from scratch in Europe, giving organizations clarity about the origins of the technology they’re building on. 

Control also extends to how AI operates inside an organization. Organizations can customize Mistral Large 4 around their proprietary data with Mistral Forge, and they can build, govern, and improve the resulting agents and applications using Mistral Studio. Mistral’s Applied AI experts can work alongside customer teams to build and deploy these tailored systems. Through that work, teams understand the architecture and decisions behind what they’ve built, along with the methods used to train and operate it, so they can run and improve their AI independently.

Sovereignty does not always require self-hosting; sometimes it just requires deployments that meet your control requirements. For organizations that prefer a managed service, Mistral Large 4 is available through Microsoft Foundry, with private deployment options for Azure developers.

Microsoft and Mistral AI share a commitment to expanding customer choice in next-generation AI. As the first cloud provider to bring Mistral Large 4 to customers, Microsoft is making Mistral’s latest open-weight model available through Microsoft Foundry, an enterprise AI platform built for evaluating, deploying, and operating models at scale. For organizations advancing sovereign AI strategies, this combination offers greater flexibility and control across their data, infrastructure, and AI operations.

Tina Schuchman, Corporate Vice President, Foundry, Microsoft

Start building with Le Chonk

Mistral Large 4 is available to try, deploy, and customize today.

Get started in Mistral Studio, through the Mistral API, or on OpenRouter. For full control, download the open weights from Hugging Face and deploy on your own infrastructure with vLLM or SGLang. The model card and license have everything you need to get started.

You can also try the new model in Vibe Code; give it a feature to build or a bug to fix in your own repository.

Mistral Large 4, is also available through NVIDIA-hosted endpoints, as an optimized NVIDIA NIM container for serving with vLLM. Developers can use the open source NeMo AutoModel library for customization or the open source TensorRT LLM library for high-throughput serving.

Enterprises can also tailor Mistral Large 4 to their proprietary data, use cases, and guardrails with Mistral Forge. Talk to our team to learn more.

The model is available to use under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight license, a modified MIT license. The model is free to use, modify, fine-tune, and commercialize, with a single condition: businesses that operate a Model-as-a-Service offering must obtain a separate commercial license from Mistral before using the model commercially.

Starting today, Mistral Large 4 is priced at $0.70 input / M, $0.07 cached input / M, and $2.10 output / M tokens.

We encourage the community to put Mistral Large 4 to the test. Run your own evaluations, push its limits, and share your findings with us on X, Discord, or GitHub.

What's Next

Mistral Large 4 will serve as the foundation for a new generation of specialized and optimized Mistral models. Building on recent releases such as Voxtral and Timestral, we'll continue expanding the frontier of open-weight AI, continuing to give developers and enterprises greater freedom to build, customize, and own their intelligence.

Andrew Prokop is a senior politics correspondent at Vox, covering the White House, elections, and political scandals and investigations. He’s worked at Vox since the site’s launch in 2014, and before that, he worked as a research assistant at the New Yorker’s Washington, DC, bureau.

When the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his “I Have a Dream” speech before huge crowds on the National Mall in August 1963, the FBI took notice.

“We must mark him now, if we have not done so before, as the most dangerous Negro of the future in this Nation from the standpoint of communism, the Negro and national security,” FBI Domestic Intelligence Chief William Sullivan wrote in a memo two days later.

A massive surveillance operation on King was quickly approved, and FBI Director J. Edgar Hoover became increasingly fixated on proving that King had communist ties and discrediting him generally.

The surveillance failed to show that King was a communist, but it did result in many tapes of extramarital sexual liaisons by King. So the next year, Sullivan sent the following unsigned letter to King's home. An unredacted version of it was only recently unearthed by Yale historian Beverly Gage, and published in the New York Times in November 2014:

According to Enemies, journalist Tim Weiner's history of the FBI, Sullivan "had a package of the King sex tapes prepared by the FBI's lab technicians," and sent it along with this letter to King's home. The package was opened by King's wife.

“You have been on the record — all your adulterous acts, your sexual orgies extending far into the past. This one is but a tiny sample,” the letter says. It threatens that the public “will know you for what you are — an evil, abnormal beast.” It continues: “Your ‘honorary’ degrees, your Nobel prize (what a grim farce) and other awards will not save you. King, I repeat you are done.”

Though the letter was unsigned and the letter writer appeared to want King to think he was black — "you know you are a complete fraud and a great liability to all of us Negroes," one line states — King and his advisers quickly concluded the letter had been sent by the FBI, Gage writes.

“There is only one thing left for you to do. You know what it is. You have just 34 days,” the letter says, apparently urging King to commit suicide. Fortunately, King didn’t back down. But the letter is a terrifying reminder of what government surveillance agencies can be capable of.

item.title: Hackers expose the identities of more than 40k DHS employees (257 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://text.npr.org/nx-s1-6021497, See on Hacker News

A hacking group cracked the U.S. Department of Homeland Security's personnel files, exposing the names, phone numbers and addresses of more than 40,000 DHS agents, operatives, and associates, on Wednesday, including those involved in undercover operations.

"On July 17th, Markwayne Mullin said he was 'turning up the heat.' This is what happens to ICE when you do that," a spokesperson for the hacktivist group behind the breach, the Department of Peace, said in an online statement.

The hackers said they stole the data by subverting DHS's single sign on system, according to an online post. It said it distributed that material to the group Distributed Denial of Secrets, which posted it online in a database called Icepick. The Department of Peace also shared the trove of data with Ryan Ottignon, a U.S.-based journalist, and a Swiss activist known as maia arson crimew. Together, the two created a searchable online database, with crimew doing all of the technical work, Ottignon told NPR.

DDoSecrets cofounder Emma Best called the leak "extraordinary but deceptive in its simplicity," because it makes explicit connections between "officials responsible for overseeing covert and undercover operations …along with key personnel in DHS's ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs."

Other activists say the information will be a boon to those investigating DHS and filing freedom of information requests, which, due to a lack of specific information, like names, email addresses, can often yield useless results.

In a statement, DHS said it was "aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively." The department added that it is taking necessary steps to "ensure all are properly protected."

More than 21,000 records identify employees with U.S. Customs and Border Protection. Another 10,000 relate to Immigration and Customs Enforcement employees and its Homeland Security Investigations unit.

It is an unprecedented breach of intelligence, coming on the heels of similar hacking attacks at the FBI. However, the database is far from comprehensive and represents about a fifth of Homeland Security's workforce, which staffs a little more than 220,000 people.

Ottignon, who has worked on similar data leak projects in the past, rejected suggestions that he and others connected to the Department of Peace or Distribution Denials of Secrets were doxing government employees.

"We are in a situation in which a group of public officials go around into cities and states and all around the country, and they seek to hide who they are. Very frequently using masks, wearing plain clothes. And they do universally unspeakable things to these communities," Ottignon said. He added that he believed that kind of behavior is unacceptable in a free society.

"We need oversight for useful government, if it exists at all. So this is just one step in that oversight process," he added.

In a note attached to the files, the Department of Peace wrote, "They have our information, so it's only fair that we have theirs."

Transcript

LEILA FADEL, HOST:

Hackers have exposed the identities of tens of thousands of Department of Homeland Security employees. That includes their names, email addresses and phone numbers. NPR immigration correspondent Vanessa Romo is covering this and joins me now. Good morning, Vanessa.

VANESSA ROMO, BYLINE: Good morning, Leila.

FADEL: So tell us about the scope of this breach.

ROMO: Well, this is a massive breach of intelligence for the government. So there is a lot of information out there. The stolen data set includes contact information for more than 41,000 DHS agents, operatives and associates, including those involved in undercover operations. And of those, more than 21,000 records identify employees with U.S. Customs and Border Protection.

Another 10,000 unmask the identities of Immigration and Customs Enforcement employees and people in Homeland Security Investigations units. And about 1,000 show people who work for the cybersecurity defense agency. That and all - a ton more are available in a searchable database. But the really interesting thing about the way the online tool works is that every personnel file includes the names of supervisors and direct reports. So you can actually follow the chain of command, which we haven't been able to see before in such an explicit way.

FADEL: A lot of information there. How did the hackers get ahold of it?

ROMO: A group of hacktivists calling themselves the Department of Peace said that they obtained the data by subverting DHS' single sign-on system. They then handed all of that raw data over to a group called Distributed Denial of Secrets - or DDoS - which partnered with a Swiss activist who goes by maia arson crimew. And that's who actually created the searchable website that's now available to the public.

FADEL: And did they say - these hackers say why they did this?

ROMO: In a note that was attached to the data, the Department of Peace basically said that it was to level the playing field. They said, quote, "they have our information, so it's only fair that we have theirs." Meanwhile, DDoS and other activists involved said that they did it as a public service so that anyone who was investigating the department can file more complete freedom of information requests.

FADEL: What about the argument that this can put ICE officers and others in danger?

ROMO: I spoke to Ryan Ottignon, a journalist who worked with the Swiss activist, crimew, to build that searchable database. And he pushed back on that idea that this was doxing.

RYAN OTTIGNON: We are in a situation in which a group of public officials go around the country, and they seek to hide who they are, very frequently using masks, and they do universally unspeakable things to these communities.

ROMO: He's referring to ICE shooting and killing Americans and noncitizens.

FADEL: Now, DHS has been aggressive about protecting ICE agents' identities. What has it said about the hack?

ROMO: So in a statement, DHS officials said the department was, quote, "aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively." They also said that they're taking necessary steps to ensure that everyone is properly protected. And as you mentioned, the Trump administration has pushed back against people publicly naming ICE agents and has regularly said that those who dox ICE officers will be prosecuted to the full extent of the law.

FADEL: That's NPR's Vanessa Romo. Thank you, Vanessa.

ROMO: Thank you, Leila.

Correction

Oct. 29th, 2026

A previous version of this story misattributed the quote, "They have our information, so it's only fair that we have theirs," to the DDoS. It was written by the Department of Peace.
