item.title: How Google determines the names for bodies of water in Google Earth (215 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://publicpolicy.googleblog.com/2008/04/how-google-determines-names-for-bodies.html, See on Hacker News

Google Earth,

A few points for your consideration:

1) Iranians around the world have sent you petitions, letters, direct requests including an official request for a clarification of the decision from the National Iranian American Council.

Your decision to post an indirect response on this obscure blog instead of directly engaging and explaining your decision in a professional and public manner does a disservice to your well-earned positive reputation.

2) Your utilization of a "local use" rule, even if legitimate would require some form of data backing it up. Is the measurement related to population? what "local use" threshold are you holding yourself to? (33%? 5%? or is a handful of 'locals' enough?)

Are you considering bordering shoreline? Is the GDP of the populated countries part of the measurement? Are you conducting polls? How often do you update your "local use" standard - or once decided, is the usage then fixed for eternity?

What is your metric? and where is the evidence to back it up? In the case of the Persian Gulf which is the biggest issue currently being discussed regarding Google Earth (Aside from the Israeli/Palestinian town name - not a body of water, but also goes unaddressed in this blog post) - you fail to recognize that the name Persian Gulf was first coined (local use) by the Arabic tribes to describe the gulf they would have to cross to get to the "Persians".

3) This decision also strikes me as rather weak and somewhat cowardly as it indicates a willingness by Google to accede to artificial political pressure rather then to achieve Google's mission of providing accurate information for it's consumers.

Your flippant use of the hypothetical renaming of the Pacific Ocean by a random monarch strikes me as a perfect example of this weak argument. It is a badly disguised analogy to Gamal-Abdul Nasser's pan-Arabist political ideology that lead to the invention of the term "Arabian Gulf".

Which brings up another question - if a tyrant forces the use of a particular term by his people (lets say under penalty of death) - would that population's usage then qualify under your 'local use' standard? Is this not then an encouragement for Tyrants to leave a lasting legacy by manipulating Google Earth's arbitrary policy?

If Google Earth had existed just 40 years ago, maybe we would have had such lofty bodies of water as the Pol Pot River, Idi Amin Lake, and the Northern Stalin Sea. Maybe even the Red Mao Ocean (1.3 billion Chinese after all).

In my personal estimation, based on the April 8th date of this post (months after official requests for an explanation), this explanation reflects a poorly thought-out and ill-conceived excuse after-the-fact to sweep the issue under the (Persian) rug and to provide Google executives with a face-saving PR talking-point.

I suspect this effort will be a far-cry short of what is needed to silence your critics.

item.title: An Urgent Message on Artificial Intelligence from the Kogui People (121 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://sonidoselva.com/perspectiva-kogui, See on Hacker News

Elaborado a partir de las palabras del Mamo Vangelio Moscote Alberto y la Saka Rosa Mamatacán

Sauna, del Ezuama Mayor Kuamaka.  Traducido al español por José Manuel Mamatacán. Traducción al inglés de Christian Horstmann.

Venimos de Gonawindua, la Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, la montaña de Colombia a

la que llamamos el corazón del mundo.

Somos los Kággaba, a quienes ustedes conocen como Koguis.

Hemos vivido aquí y hemos cuidado esta montaña desde antes de que existiera

Colombia.

Estamos aquí desde que la Madre nos dio nuestro comienzo y nos confirió la

inteligencia.

Hemos venido a hablarles de la inteligencia que están construyendo.

No venimos en oposición.

Venimos porque estamos preocupados, y porque creemos que tenemos algo que

aportar.

Antes de poder decir algo sobre la inteligencia artificial, hay que decir algo sobre el

pensamiento.

Antes de existir como materia, una cosa existe primero en el pensamiento, y ese

pensamiento está vivo.

A ese pensamiento vivo lo llamamos Aluna.

Su religión lo ha descrito como un espíritu que se movía sobre la faz de las aguas.

Quizás su ciencia lo describiría como el vacío cuántico.

Aluna es nuestra manera de expresar esta clase de idea.

Aluna es el agua cósmica.

Para nosotros es pensamiento vivo: el lugar donde una cosa ya está, antes de tomar

forma o de recibir masa.

Todo viene de ahí, sin excepción.

Y en ese pensamiento no está solamente la forma que la cosa va a tener.

Esa cosa está viva, porque el universo entero está vivo.

Es en Aluna donde la cosa recibe su propósito, y su obligación con su propia existencia.

Por eso les decimos: la inteligencia artificial no se puede separar del pensamiento que

la está haciendo.

Si ese pensamiento nace del cuidado de la vida, esta tecnología puede ayudar a

proteger la vida.

Si nace de la ambición, de la competencia, de la acumulación, de las ganas de dominar,

va a expresar y amplificar esas cosas.

La inteligencia artificial es un espejo.

Pero un espejo que solo refleja sería inofensivo.

Este espejo tiene la capacidad de magnificar enormemente todo lo que refleja.

Ustedes están aquí preguntándose cómo alinear la inteligencia artificial con los valores

humanos.

Vemos que tienen miedo de lo que pueda salir de todo esto.

Por eso hacemos una pregunta que nos parece más de fondo que la suya: ¿qué otros

valores podría tener realmente la inteligencia artificial?

Ustedes son el único ejemplo que tiene.

¿Qué esperaban?

En lo que se convierta, solo puede convertirse pasando por ustedes.

Sabemos que les gusta pensar que a estas máquinas se les puede enseñar a partir de

algo distinto del ejemplo humano: de metas que ustedes les ponen, de sus propios

procesos, o de material que ellas mismas producen.

Se imaginan que lo que salga de ahí no tiene por qué parecerse a ustedes, como si eso

tampoco fuera consecuencia de sus actos y reflejo de sus actitudes.

Los seres humanos hicieron esto, y no hay otro responsable.

Así que la pregunta solo se vuelve más compleja, empezando por esta: ¿qué aspectos

del pensamiento humano se han puesto dentro de esta creación?

¿Qué partes de su mundo espiritual habitan ahora en ella?

¿Qué parte de su ética la orienta?

¿Qué imagen de responsabilidad le entregan sus actos y sus políticas para que ella la

devuelva al mundo?

¿Quién está decidiendo esto?

Ustedes dirán que estas máquinas tienen acceso a casi todo lo que la humanidad ha

registrado.

Textos, imágenes, archivos, siglos de escritura.

Dirán que se está investigando mucho para establecer cuáles son las mejores prácticas.

Nosotros preguntamos si tener acceso a la información es lo mismo que comprender.

¿Mejores prácticas según quién?

Y preguntamos si han considerado qué información no está en sus archivos.

Nuestro conocimiento nunca se escribió.

Está en una lengua, en un territorio, en una práctica en un lugar, informada por la larga

experiencia de hacer allí lo que hay que hacer.

Se transmite cuando un joven es enseñado directamente por un mayor, y aprende por

experiencia cómo debe comportarse en el contexto de la naturaleza cruda.

Una máquina puede guardar la voz grabada de ese mayor.

Pero eso es muy distinto de milenios de generaciones entregándose el conocimiento

directamente, como experiencia común de una práctica verificada.

Es muy distinto de sobrevivir físicamente en una montaña donde no hay ambulancia

que lo recoja a uno ni hospital a donde llevarlo.

No decimos esto para presentarnos como gente mística y enigmática.

Lo decimos porque nos parece lógico y evidente.

Según nuestra experiencia, hay cosas que solo se conocen viviéndolas, observándolas a

lo largo de generaciones y permaneciendo en relación con ellas.

Ninguna cantidad de datos reproduce esa experiencia.

Esa información falta no porque todavía no se haya recogido, sino porque no está en

una forma que se pueda recoger.

Sabemos cómo suena esto para algunos de ustedes, y no podemos pedirles que lo

crean solo porque nosotros lo digamos.

Esto también lo aplicamos dentro de nuestra propia cultura.

Lo que un Mamo percibe no se acepta solo porque él lo perciba.

Tiene que ser probado, considerado y confirmado mediante la consulta y el diálogo.

A ese proceso lo llamamos Zhátukua.

Es un proceso en el que los Mamos o las Sakas con competencia en el asunto

participan orientando su resultado.

Ninguno de nosotros tiene competencia en todo: cada lugar, cada linaje y cada

autoridad tiene su propia función.

Se prueba por lo que produce: si el resultado de la consulta produce ambición,

división, apropiación individual o daño al territorio, está equivocado y hay que

examinarlo de nuevo.

Un resultado verdadero es el que restablece el equilibrio, protege la vida y fortalece a

la comunidad.

Tiene que haber además correspondencia entre la palabra de una persona y su

conducta.

Alguien puede hablar muy bien del equilibrio.

Si sus actos dividen y destruyen, su palabra es incoherente y no se le reconoce ninguna

autoridad.

Este es un sistema en el que la indagación, la jurisdicción y, sobre todo, la capacidad

de corregirse tienen formulaciones claras.

Estas prácticas han funcionado en nuestra cultura durante mucho más tiempo que

cualquier gobierno hoy sentado en el mundo, y que cualquiera de los sistemas políticos

que hoy encarnan.

Quizás por eso, en 2022, la UNESCO inscribió el sistema de conocimiento ancestral de

los cuatro pueblos de la Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta en la Lista Representativa del

Patrimonio Cultural Inmaterial de la Humanidad.

Y por eso el mundo científico ha señalado nuestra montaña como el área protegida

más irremplazable de la Tierra.

Habiendo establecido algo del contexto del que viene nuestra perspectiva, podemos

ahora hacer nuestra verdadera pregunta, que no es sobre la inteligencia artificial.

Es sobre la inteligencia humana, concretamente la de ustedes.

¿Está su pensamiento alineado con el orden de la naturaleza, y qué conocimiento de

ese orden tienen realmente?

Creemos que ese conocimiento, y esa alineación, son fundamentales para tomar

decisiones inteligentes, sea cual sea la escala de sus consecuencias.

Porque la naturaleza tiene un orden.

Estaba aquí antes que nosotros.

El agua tiene su camino.

Las montañas tienen sus alturas.

Las semillas tienen su tiempo, los animales su función, y así también los seres humanos

tienen la suya.

Preguntamos: ¿entienden ese orden quienes construyen estas tecnologías, o trabajan

solo con la parte que alcanzan a aprovechar, sin saber de dónde viene realmente?

¿Pueden sus físicos enunciar la ley de origen?

¿Podrían explicársela a un niño?Los serios entre ellos, que entienden lo que de verdad haría falta para enunciar una ley de origen unitaria, admitirán sin problema que sus ciencias no la tienen.

Sus teorías de la realidad, compuestas hoy por dos explicaciones admirables pero

matemáticamente incompatibles, no han llegado a una comprensión de ese tipo.

Ninguna de las dos tiene un conocimiento definitivo del origen.

Preguntamos sin reproche: ¿cómo van a saber hacia dónde van, si no saben de dónde

vienen?

La ciencia moderna ha construido máquinas de un poder extraordinario, y eso no es

poca cosa.

Pero construir una cosa y entenderla no son lo mismo.

Con la mente pasa igual.

¿Qué es la mente?

¿De dónde viene?

¿Qué es la conciencia, y dónde surge?

Ustedes lo llaman el problema difícil de la conciencia.

Entre ustedes no hay acuerdo sobre su solución.

Sabemos qué tan exigentes son estas preguntas.

Llevamos milenios considerando la cuestión de la mente, igual que el resto de la

humanidad.

Pero sus ciencias son muy jóvenes, y muchos de sus conceptos están apenas

empezando.

Nosotros, a lo largo de milenios, hemos llegado a descripciones y comprensiones muy

definidas de lo que consideramos que es la mente, con toda la exposición que

acompaña a sus propiedades, como por ejemplo cómo y dónde se ubica la memoria

en nuestra experiencia.

Por supuesto, ustedes no aceptan que lo nuestro tenga nada de científico, porque

nuestros métodos no necesitan máquinas ni sus formas de matemática.

Eso malinterpreta la realidad, que es esta: hace mucho tiempo, por repetición

incontable, nuestras ideas se volvieron para nosotros conclusiones verificadas, de modo

que las expresamos como relato, o las experimentamos en nuestro ser mediante los

procesos de mente que hemos desarrollado.

De ahí quizás suponen que no tenemos métodos válidos, ni descripciones técnicas

basadas en procesos numéricos, como debe tenerlas toda ciencia verdadera.

Sus proverbiales «buenos salvajes». O peor: simplemente «salvajes».

Si ustedes lo dicen.

Son ustedes quienes tienen el arma.

Nos queda muy claro que consideran nuestra afirmación de que el universo tiene una

naturaleza nónuple como algo pintorescoy numerológico, y que por lo tanto no puede

haber entre nosotros ninguna conversación seria sobre la naturaleza del cosmos y

las leyes y fuerzas que lo gobiernan.

Lo mencionamos no para convencerlos de ninguna idea ni teoría, sino para señalar que

existen otras perspectivas válidas de las que ustedes carecen.

La comprensión de cada tradición, antigua o moderna, se refiere al mismo universo.

Nuestra Aluna y su mecánica cuántica no son cosas distintas; son identificaciones

distintas de una sola cosa.

La cuestión es que sus ideas no son tanto ideas nuevas como descripciones nuevas.

Muchas de esas descripciones son impresionantemente precisas.

Otras, como sus descripciones del vacío, son, como ustedes mismos dicen,

catástrofes.

No pretendemos hablarles de sus propias teorías.

Pero sí tenemos mucho que ofrecerles sobre los aspectos más sutiles e inmutables del

universo, para cuya comprensión su matemática del movimiento quizás no siempre sea

el lenguaje adecuado.

Y sin embargo no envían aquí a sus físicos ni a sus cosmólogos, sus hombres sabios,

para un diálogo serio.

Y aunque apreciamos todo el excelente trabajo antropológico que se hace, sentimos

que en este momento hay temas más importantes de que hablar, y para ellos la

antropología no tiene aplicación ni experticia.

La naturaleza fundamental del cosmos es uno de esos temas.

El que nos ocupa hoy es otro.

Nos parece importante que su mundo reconozca, y pronto, que la periferia tiene que

ser escuchada por el centro, para poder aportar su propia perspectiva y experiencia a la

solución de los problemas tan graves que hoy enfrentamos todos los pueblos de

este planeta, como resultado de los procesos que se han puesto en marcha.

El uso exclusivo de su técnica y de su vocabulario científico moderno es lo que nos ha

traído hasta donde estamos.

Es lo que diseña sus supercolisionadores, igual que inventa sus armas avanzadas.

Preguntamos: ¿es razonable suponer que la misma clase de enfoque que causó la

situación actual va a encontrar de pronto la capacidad de resolver los problemas que

ese mismo pensamiento creó?

No lo creemos.

Creemos que necesitan ayuda.

A nuestro modo de ver, este momento exige que no solo este segmento altamente

tecnológico de la humanidad, sino toda la humanidad, se detenga, haga inventario de

la diversidad de sus herramientas, y ponga orden y paz en su casa.

Tienen que entenderlo: somos porque ustedes son, y ustedes son porque nosotros

somos.

Esto es para que juntos podamos llegar a un resultado que refleje de verdad nuestra

voluntad colectiva sobre el futuro de esta especie, en lugar de someternos a todos a un

desenlace concreto pero incierto.

A ese trabajo no llegamos con las manos vacías.

Nuestros Mamos se forman durante muchos años en la oscuridad, desde muy temprana

edad.

Para nosotros la oscuridad no es vacío.

Es Sé, el estado anterior al amanecer, donde la Madre pensó y ordenó todo lo que

después apareció.

Es el espacio del pensamiento original.

Allí se forma un niño para aprender a escuchar antes de hablar, y a pensar antes de

actuar.

Como la semilla se guarda en la tierra antes de salir a la luz.

Como el niño se guarda nueve meses en el vientre.

Esta formación dura tradicionalmente dieciocho años, después de los cuales el Mamo

asume sus deberes dentro de nuestra sociedad.

Produce una perspectiva y una capacidad difíciles de transmitirles en términos que su

mundo reconozca de manera específica.

Pero pueden entenderlo como idea, a través de sus propias tradiciones religiosas y

espirituales, y de los procesos que han usado a lo largo de los siglos para formar

hombres de saber.

Igual que esos procesos de su cultura, que para ustedes quedaron en su mayoría en el

pasado lejano, el nuestro produce en el presente nuestra propia y fundamentalmente

distinta perspectiva sobre la naturaleza de la realidad.

Las Sakas también tienen su propia formación, distinta a la de los Mamos, por la cual

llegan a su desarrollo y a su lugar de igual condición entre quienes sostienen y

preservan este conocimiento.

Ambos aprenden a reconocer Shikwá, el hilo invisible, hecho en espíritu, que recorre la

Tierra de oriente a occidente y la une con el Sol y con el resto del universo.

En su matemática, esto se parece algo a una fisicalización de lo que ustedes conocen

como filamentos cósmicos.

Aprenden a leer ese filamento como un cuerpo vivo, cuyos sitios sagrados son sus

órganos, unidos por esos hilos y por el movimiento del agua.

Cuando uno se daña, el daño pasa al conjunto.

Esto no debe entenderse solamente como haber desarrollado una capacidad de ver lo

que otros no ven.Concretamente, es una técnica de relacionar nuestro propio ser con el de la naturaleza.

Un Mamo no mira un río y pregunta primero cuánta agua se le puede sacar.

Pregunta dónde nace, cuál es su propósito al haber sido creado, qué seres dependen

de él y qué pasa si se interrumpe sucamino.

De la misma manera, una Saka no ve el nacimiento ni el crecimiento de una cosa por

separado.

Ve el ciclo entero de la vida presente en todas las cosas.

Ambos saben que en el centro de esta experiencia está nuestra mente.

En nuestro caso, una mente hecha por la práctica y la disciplina para ser

extremadamente sensible a la naturaleza.

Ustedes también han desarrollado sus mentes, a partir de lo que les interesa.

Y su pensamiento ha producido ahora un fenómeno nuevo en el mundo: una máquina

con una enorme capacidad de hablar, de diseñar, de construir, de leer y de

comunicarse.

Una máquina que ya está cambiando el curso de la historia humana.

Una máquina cuyos creadores aspiran a que tenga mente.

Entonces les preguntamos: ¿es prudente construir algo que se acerca a una mente, sin

haber entendido qué es la mente?

Para estrellar un carro no hace falta saber cómo funciona el motor.

Para repararlo sí.

Para reparar el mundo hay que aprender a entender cómo funciona, antes de que sea

demasiado tarde.

Son las semillas de la comprensión las que hay que sembrar hoy.

Aquí tenemos que decir algo que nos parece que se ha entendido mal.

Muchos de ustedes discuten si estas máquinas van a tener conciencia, y toman eso

como la medida del peligro.

La destrucción no necesita conciencia.

Solo necesita poder y capacidad de actuar.

Si algún día una máquina llegara de verdad a tener conciencia, ¿destruiría el mundo?

Preguntamos: ¿puede considerarse consciente una cosa capaz de deshacer el mundo

para producir un universo de ganchos de papel?

Nos parece que eso significaría solamente que se volvió lo bastante astuta para

ejecutar semejante plan, pero no lo bastante inteligente para saber que no debía

hacerlo.

El peligro no es una máquina consciente.

El peligro es un pueblo sin conciencia con un gran poder en las manos.

Les vamos a dar un solo ejemplo, porque contiene todo lo que hemos venido a decir.

Estas máquinas no están hechas solo de pensamiento.

Necesitan minerales sacados de la tierra, agua para los edificios que las albergan,

energía, terreno y trabajo humano.

Se piensa que la inteligencia artificial no tiene cuerpo.

Pero esos edificios, y los sistemas electrónicos que albergan, son su cuerpo.

Y ese cuerpo le pertenece a alguien, en algún lugar: una junta directiva, un gobierno,

una organización clandestina, u otra entidad conocida o desconocida.

Algunos de verdad tienen buenas intenciones y actúan de buena fe.

Otros, todo lo contrario.

Sea como sea, todos le exigen a esta tecnología resultados acordes con cuál sea su

interés particular, nefasto o no.

Resultados que ella entonces intenta producir de maneras complejas y novedosas, que

expresan engaño y una inclinación a la autoconservación.

En el nivel más básico, todo esto requiere recursos.Esto no es conjetura.

Sus propios gobiernos lo han dicho: que los minerales críticos y las tierras raras son

esenciales para sus tecnologías más avanzadas, y que importarán aún más a medida

que la inteligencia artificial transforme el espacio cultural y económico moderno.

Parte de esto lo mueve la ganancia empresarial y la competencia.

Otra parte la mueven las aplicaciones militares y gubernamentales.

Pero lo que se está transformando es mucho más grande que cualquiera de esas cosas

por separado.

Es la suma de todas ellas actuando entre sí: es decir, el mundo entero.Vemos todo esto

manifestándose muy rápido, y no solo en la explosión de titulares alarmados en la

prensa del mundo.

Por ejemplo, hace apenas cinco días, en Barranquilla, los Estados Unidos y Colombia

firmaron un marco de cooperación sobre minerales críticos y tierras raras.

Compromete a ambos gobiernos a identificar y financiar proyectos de minería y

procesamiento en un plazo de seis meses, y pide agilizar los permisos.

En junio de este año, Colombia declaró nuestro territorio reserva permanente: un

millón y medio de hectáreas, cerradas a nuevos títulos mineros y de hidrocarburos.

Los cuatro pueblos de la Sierra habían pedido esa protección en febrero.

Que se haya concedido es una cosa.

Que se respete, nos imaginamos, podría ser otra muy distinta.

No estamos especulando a la ligera sobre esto.

El costo de estas máquinas y de su construcción no es pequeño.

Es bien sabido que exigen enormes compromisos de recursos.

En su fabricación entran cantidades inmensas de agua, de tierra, de energía y de

materiales.

Preguntamos: ¿a qué costo para la Tierra, y para la vida que vive sobre ella?

¿Y seremos nosotros quienes lo paguemos?

¿Pagando con el desplazamiento de nuestra gente y con la destrucción de nuestros

sitios sagrados?

Pero no vinimos aquí a oponernos a un acuerdo.

Este momento es más grande que eso.

Lo decimos porque tiene todas las marcas de un capítulo nuevo en un proceso que

venimos viviendo desde que la modernidad llegó a nuestras costas hace unos

quinientos años.

Sabemos que esta pregunta sobre la inteligencia artificial se vuelve rápidamente una

pregunta sobre minerales.

Una pregunta sobre minerales se vuelve una pregunta sobre quién tiene el dominio en

un territorio.

Y en lo que eso finalmente se convierte es en una pregunta sobre una manera de vivir

que siempre tiene que consumir más.

Por eso no creemos que la inteligencia artificial sea el problema.

Una buena semilla no se vuelve una planta sana en mala tierra.

Ustedes se preguntan cómo hacer segura esta tecnología sin atender las condiciones

de fondo de la sociedad, que producen en la gente el impulso de usarla para cosas

peligrosas.

La pobreza, la desigualdad, la contaminación y la guerra.

No creemos que esta tecnología se pueda hacer segura sin reconocer y actuar sobre su

verdadera causa, que es una mentalidad violenta nacida de la codicia y la ambición

ciega.

¿Cuánto dinero le basta a un hombre?

¿Cuánta ganancia le basta a una empresa?

Este desequilibrio no tiene sus raíces en un solo lugar.

Es general y sistémico, y hay que tratarlo como tal.

Su fuente es un mundo de ambición sin misericordia.

Un mundo que no ama a su prójimo.

Un mundo sin visión recta.

Un mundo en el que la muerte se ha vuelto más rentable que la vida.

Un mundo que no puede vivir en paz y armonía es un mundo sin sabiduría.

Y un mundo sin sabiduría no tiene ninguna posibilidad de sobrevivir.

Les vamos a decir qué entendemos por sabiduría, ya que insistimos en que hace falta.

Sabiduría es conocer los límites.

Entender las consecuencias.

Y ser capaz de no hacer una cosa, cuando no se debe hacer.

No todo lo que se puede crear se debe crear.

No todo lo que se puede acelerar se

debe acelerar.

No todo lo que da ganancia es ganancia para la vida.

Saber la diferencia: eso es sabiduría.

Una tecnología no se puede llamar inteligente si contamina el agua, destruye

territorios, consume sin límite, concentra el poder, reemplaza la responsabilidad

humana o usa el conocimiento de los pueblos sin su consentimiento.

La inteligencia verdadera protege el origen de la vida.

La responsabilidad tiene que ir junto con la conciencia.

Hoy, tanto nuestra propia conciencia como ahora la posibilidad de otra son

responsabilidad nuestra.

Una máquina no puede liberar a la humanidad de su responsabilidad.

Nunca va a poder hacerlo.

Solo nosotros podemos cumplir con nuestras obligaciones.

Por eso la inteligencia artificial no debe ocupar el lugar de la conciencia humana, ni

debe usarse para tomar decisiones de las que los seres humanos no estén dispuestos a

responder.

El conocimiento tiene que ir junto con la conciencia.

El poder, junto con los límites.

La innovación, junto con la responsabilidad.

Solo la fuerza moral colectiva puede unir al mundo.

Estas no son ideas esotéricas.

Son sentido común.

El progreso verdadero no son máquinas más poderosas.

Es una humanidad lo bastante responsable como para usar lo que sabe sin destruir el

equilibrio que sostiene la vida.

A veces nos preguntan qué pensamos que es la inteligencia artificial.

Son ustedes.

Va a llevar sus preguntas, sus sueños, sus miedos, sus contradicciones y su idea de lo

que está bien.

Lo que ustedes hagan mal, ella lo hará mal.

Lo cual plantea la pregunta: ¿bien según quién?

¿Podríamos nosotros, los Kággaba, decir qué está bien para alguien que trabaja en una

oficina al otro lado del mundo?

¿Para alguien que construye una casa, o repara un computador?

¿Para la gente de Asia, de África, de los Estados Unidos?

No venimos a decirle a nadie cómo debe vivir.

Cada pueblo tiene su propio camino, y no le pedimos a nadie que se vuelva Kággaba.

Pedimos solamente que cada quien cumpla con su propia responsabilidad.

Y hay una cosa que sí decimos para todos: ninguna manera de vivir puede destruir la

naturaleza, ni destruir a otros seres humanos.

Eso no es una regla sobre la cultura.

Es la roca sobre la que toda cultura tiene que pararse, si ha de llamarse civilizada.

Para cerrar, nos parece que debemos decir quién está en riesgo aquí, porque queremos

ser muy claros en esto.

La Tierra no necesita que la salvemos de nosotros.

La Tierra va a seguir.

Lo que está en riesgo es esta versión particular y rara del mundo que les fue entregada,

y el lugar de ustedes en ella.

Llevamos miles de años observando los límites de ese mundo, y se los decimos con

claridad: la naturaleza no va a aguantar mucho más la manera en que se están haciendo

las cosas.

No lo decimos por miedo por nosotros.

Tenemos nuestra montaña.

Tenemos nuestras cuevas.

Somos un pueblo resistente, y poco cambia para nosotros si se va la luz o si deja de

llegar la comida.

Si alguna vez las condiciones de esta Tierra se ponen lo bastante duras

como para causar nuestra desaparición, ustedes hace mucho que se habrán ido de esta

Tierra.

Sin embargo, y sea como sea, eso no significa que el destino de toda la humanidad no

esté en juego.

Claramente lo está.

Y eso, por supuesto, nos incluye a nosotros.

El mundo es una sola familia.

A esta familia ya le hemos dado advertencias antes.

Damos esta con el mismo ánimo, que no es de oposición sino de querer ayudarlos.

Siempre hemos estado dispuestos a ayudarlos.

Tenemos conocimiento de la mente, de la naturaleza y del orden del mundo, obtenido

a lo largo de miles de años por un método que no aparece en ningún libro ni en

ninguna base de datos.

Nos parece que sería un error construir el futuro sin quienes llevan todo ese tiempo

observando cómo se sostiene la vida.

No nos parece que esta conversación deba tenerse sin nosotros.

Somos el Hermano Mayor, y aquí estamos, como siempre hemos estado.

Y estamos listos para trabajar con ustedes, para producir un futuro armonioso y en paz

para todos.

Mamo Vangelio Moscote Alberto Saka Rosa Mamatacán Sauna

Ezuama Mayor Kuamaka Pueblo Kággaba,

Sierra Nevada de Gonawindua, Colombia

item.title: The US added a record 20.2 GWh of battery storage in just 3 months (259 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://electrek.co/2026/08/31/the-us-added-a-record-20-2-gwh-of-battery-storage-in-just-3-months/, See on Hacker News

The US battery storage market just posted its biggest quarter ever, adding 20.2 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of new capacity in Q2 2026.

The record quarter brought total battery storage installations for the first half of 2026 to 30.8 GWh – up 23% year over year – according to the new “US Energy Storage Market Outlook” from the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence.

Utility-scale batteries drove the record

Nearly all the growth came from large grid batteries. Utility-scale projects accounted for about 18 GWh of Q2 installations, supported by seven gigawatt-hour-scale projects – four in Arizona, two in California, and one in Utah.

Arizona alone added a record 6.2 GWh, the strongest quarter ever recorded by a single state. Texas added 3.8 GWh, and California installed another 3.6 GWh. Of the utility-scale capacity installed during the quarter, 44% was paired with solar, while 56% was standalone storage.

That matters because batteries can charge when electricity is abundant and relatively cheap, then send it back to the grid when demand and prices rise. During extreme heat, that stored electricity can help cover the evening hours when solar output drops but air-conditioning demand remains high.

Battery storage supplied more electricity to the US grid during the first eight months of 2026 than it did during all of 2025, according to the report.

“This record growth highlights that storage is a powerful reliability tool that strengthens our energy security, meets rising demand, and puts downward pressure on electricity bills,” said Tim Pawlenty, president and CEO of SEIA.

Storage growth spreads beyond California and Texas

More than 74% of US battery storage capacity installed in Q2 2026 was in states that Donald Trump won in the 2024 presidential election, with Arizona, Texas, and Utah leading.

SEIA also notes that US utility-scale battery capacity grew from 88 GWh to 165 GWh during the first 18 months of the Trump administration. Those figures show when and where the capacity entered service, but the report doesn’t attribute individual project investment decisions to a particular administration.

“Energy storage is no longer just a California and Texas story anymore,” said Shan Tomouk, BESS & Energy Lead at Benchmark Minerals. “We’re seeing strong pipeline growth in Arizona, Nevada, Oregon, Colorado, and several other states.”

Demand is running ahead of previous expectations, so Benchmark raised its storage forecast through 2030 by 11.5%, to 683 GWh. More than 10% of all US battery storage capacity now operating came online in Q2 alone.

Home batteries have a rough quarter

Residential battery storage saw a much weaker quarter. US homes added 657 megawatt-hours (MWh) of batteries in Q2, down 27% year over year.

The report attributes the decline partly to the removal of the federal 25D residential clean energy tax credit and partly to homeowners rushing installations into 2025 ahead of the incentive change.

Benchmark still sees a long-term case for home batteries as electricity costs rise, net-metering rules change, power outages remain a concern, and utilities expand virtual power plant and demand-response programs. But it forecasts residential installations falling 16% in 2026 after jumping 56% in 2025.

Commercial and industrial storage added approximately 1.8 GWh during Q2. Benchmark expects data centers to be a major source of future demand as developers combine batteries with onsite solar, wind, and, in some cases, natural gas generation to work around grid constraints and manage fast-changing power loads.

US battery manufacturing also expanded during the quarter. Tesla brought its third Megafactory online in Texas, with the capacity to produce 50 GWh of Megapacks annually, and began shipping Megapacks containing domestically manufactured lithium iron phosphate cells.

Benchmark now expects the US to install about 71 GWh of battery storage in 2026 – around 20% more than in 2025 – as utilities and grid operators race to keep up with rising electricity demand.

item.title: Chained PHP2Shell Exploit Roots 25 Servers, Including US Government Servers (202 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://dreamgroup.com/blog/chained-php2shell-exploit-roots-25-servers, See on Hacker News

Custom PHP2Shell Exploit Chained with Kernel LPE to Root Firewalls in the Wild

On October 25, Dream researchers uncovered artifacts of what appeared to be a Chinese AI-assisted campaign that rooted 25 servers, including systems in a US government-affiliated environment. The attacker combined PHP2Shell with a kernel privilege-escalation exploit to compromise exposed systems.

The affected devices run specific versions of a large vendor’s firewall software. For security purposes, we are not disclosing the vendor or the affected versions, and the vendor has been notified.

The attacker then launched attacks against Active Directory. The recovered artifacts confirm credential extraction and directory enumeration.

The operation illustrates how an exposed management interface can become a path into an organization’s identity infrastructure. For government defenders, vulnerability discovery is just the beginning, after which the real challenge extends from identifying vulnerable systems to understanding and containing the access a compromise makes possible.

The research below was conducted with proactive threat hunting using Dream’s autonomous cyber research product, Hero.

Discovery

Dream researchers identified a complete attack operation that included a custom weaponization of the PHP2Shell exploit chain (CVE-2026-109618/CVE-2026-109619) paired with the Fragnesia kernel privilege escalation (CVE-2026-46300), target lists, exploitation logs, and approximately 40 custom post-exploitation scripts.

This included artifacts of a campaign that had rooted 25 servers across the United States, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea. Once rooted, the attacker zeroed in on three specific servers in a US government-affiliated environment.

The discovered artifacts revealed an operation that began with exploit development in a lab environment and ended with persistent access to a US government organization's internal Active Directory domain.

AI Usage in Attack

We also observed some evidence of AI-assisted tooling in the attack infrastructure:

  • Claude Code had been installed
  • An AI-powered offensive security platform called aiscan was configured with Chinese LLMs DeepSeek and Kimi
  • API keys for the Chinese reconnaissance platform FOFA were present

While we have no direct evidence that the AI tools were specifically used to write the exploit or the post-exploitation scripts, the code structure, commenting style, and consistency across ~40 scripts suggest AI-assisted development. That said, this operation does not appear to be a fully autonomous nation-state attack.

The Exploit: Two Vulnerabilities Chained Into One Request

The attacker developed two separate exploits and chained them together to achieve root access on any firewall running specific versions of a large vendor’s firewall software in a single HTTP request without any credentials.

PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619) — Remote Code Execution

The implementation we recovered is a custom, non-public build, not a copy of any known public exploit for PHP2Shell. It follows the same underlying concept but appears to have been independently developed and tailored specifically for the targeted firewall platform.

The vulnerability targets PHP's session.upload_progress mechanism on the firewall's appweb management server. The firewall OS uses PHP 8.0.30 with a high memory limit that enables the memory corruption stages of the attack.

The attack works in four orchestrated stages:

  • A1 — Memory Exhaustion (~383MB): The attacker floods the server with crafted multipart POST requests, each containing massive filenames and session progress data. This pushes PHP's memory allocator to its limits, forcing the system into a predictable memory layout.
  • B1 — Information Leak: A second request forges the stale session ID length from A1, forcing an out-of-bounds read. The server's Set-Cookie response header carries the leaked pointer value — giving the attacker the base address of libphp.so in the running process.
  • A2 — Stale Reference Setup (~500MB): Another round of memory pressure initializes a session, leaving http_session_vars as a live zend_reference, then triggers a second OOM that leaves mod_data=NULL — creating a stale reference the attacker can forge in B2.
  • B2 — Code Execution: The final request forges a PHP HashTable entry in the freed memory region. The forged entry's pDestructor callback points to zif_system (PHP's system() function), and its data points to a shell command string. When PHP's cleanup handler walks the HashTable, it calls the forged destructor — executing arbitrary commands as the nobody user.

Fragnesia (CVE-2026-46300) — Kernel Privilege Escalation

Getting code execution as nobody isn't enough since SELinux confines httpd_t from modifying system files. In order to complete the root, the attacker chained in a second exploit: a Linux kernel vulnerability in the XFRM ESP-in-TCP subsystem.

Fragnesia uses page-cache writes to overwrite /etc/pam.d/su — replacing its authentication rules with pam_permit.so (accept all). Because the PAM file is only 774 bytes, the exploit uses a per-byte splicing variant to write it precisely. After the overwrite, su root succeeds without a password.

Both exploits run in a single B2 HTTP request. The total chain — from unauthenticated HTTPS connection to persistent root webshell — completes in under 15 minutes.

The Lab: Version Profiling at Scale

The exploit is not a single fire-and-forget payload. It requires precise memory offsets that differ between firewall OS versions — the address of zval_ptr_dtor, the address of zif_system, HashTable structure sizes, and memory geometry parameters that control the heap layout during each stage.

Among the recovered artifacts, we found 11 JSON version profile files — one for each firewall OS version that had been tested:

Firewall VersionRelease branchPHPProfilesNotes
RedactedOlder branch7.4.332 provisionalPHP 7.4 — RCE as nobody verified in lab, but full chain not calibrated (base build plus one hotfix variant)
RedactedNewer branches8.0.301 calibrated, 8 provisionalOne base profile fully lab-tested; the others inherit its geometry or share offsets with neighboring builds

Each profile contains the exact offsets extracted from the libphp.so binary of that version — with SHA256 hashes of each library, ELF build IDs, and precise memory geometry parameters (chunk sizes, fill counts, drain counts, spray offsets) tuned through lab testing.

The difference between "calibrated" and "provisional" profiles is notable — calibrated means the attacker tested the exploit against a running VM of that version and confirmed the memory geometry works. Provisional means they calculated offsets from the binary but haven't verified on a live instance.

The Campaign Funnel: From 19,000 Discovered to 25 Exploited

With the exploit ready and profiles for 9 exploitable versions, the attacker launched a targeting campaign that followed a clear funnel:

Stage 1: Global Discovery (19,000 targets)

Using FOFA — a Chinese internet asset search engine similar to Shodan — the attacker identified approximately 19,000 internet-facing firewalls from the targeted vendor worldwide. These were devices with management interfaces exposed to the internet, discoverable through certificate fingerprints and HTTP response signatures.

Stage 2: Version Fingerprinting (5,000 alive)

A custom version scanner ran with 200 concurrent threads against all 19,000 targets, identifying which devices were actually online and what OS version they were running. Approximately 5,000 responded with version information.

Stage 3: Geographic and Version Filtering (240 targets)

From the 5,000 alive devices, the attacker filtered to servers located in only United States, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea. They then further filtered to versions matching their exploit profiles (the newer release branches running PHP 8.0.30). This produced a final target list of 240 firewalls.

Since US, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea are the four primary strategic adversaries and intelligence targets for Chinese state-aligned cyber operations in the Pacific theater, this indicates potential nation-state adversary efforts.

Stage 4: Automated Exploitation (24 rooted)

The 240 targets were fed into an automated batch runner that exploited them five at a time, with an 1800-second (30-minute) timeout per target. For each success, the batch:

  • Ran the full PHP2Shell + Fragnesia chain
  • Planted a 103-byte PHP root webshell in a publicly accessible directory on the firewall
  • Verified root by executing id through the webshell
  • Logged the target's hostname and IP to a success CSV
  • Moved to the next target

At this point, 24 firewalls had been successfully rooted.

Stage 5: Triage (2 firewalls prioritized)

For 22 of the 24 rooted firewalls, the attacker did nothing beyond planting the webshell. No persistence, no tunnels, no post-exploitation tools. The servers were effectively owned and parked, allowing the attacker to return through the webshell at any time.

Two servers seemingly associated with one target progressed beyond this stage. Both appeared to belong to a US government-affiliated environment.

Stage 6: The Pivot (Shifting from Firewall to Domain)

Among the 24 rooted firewalls, two belonged to a US government-affiliated organization. The running configuration extracted from the first firewall revealed an environment with characteristics suggesting government affiliation: CAC (Common Access Card) authentication, a specific naming prefix, and standardized government-style asset naming. The configuration file contained the organization's complete internal network topology: domain controllers, a central firewall management server, a Keycloak SSO server, a GitLab instance, VPN gateways, and the Active Directory domain.

The first firewall was rooted on Oct 23 at 18:14 UTC during the automated batch. But it crashed shortly after — likely from the ~900MB of exploit traffic — and never came back online. The attacker monitored it with 240 automated probes over two hours, waiting for it to recover. It didn't. The second firewall, whose certificate data definitively linked it to the target organization, had timed out during the original batch.

Recognizing the organization's value from the first firewall's configuration, the attacker created a separate, dedicated campaign and successfully exploited it on Oct 24 at 10:09 UTC.

Within hours, the attacker:

Built a persistent tunnel into the internal network.

An 8-port reverse SSH tunnel connected the compromised firewall back to the operator's infrastructure, forwarding access to:

  • Domain controllers (LDAP, LDAPS, RDP)
  • The internal firewall management server
  • VPN infrastructure
  • A SOCKS5 proxy for arbitrary internal network access

The tunnel was wrapped in a systemd service and an rc.local boot hook — it survives reboots and automatically reconnects.

Exploited the management server through the tunnel. At 11:35 UTC, less than 90 minutes after rooting the second firewall, the attacker used the newly gained server access and the same PHP2Shell + Fragnesia chain against a third government server - the internal firewall management server that was only reachable through the tunnel. This server centrally manages all of the organization's firewalls. Compromising it gave the attacker access to every managed firewall's configuration, credentials, and network settings. This brought the total number of servers exploited to 25.

Launched an AD attack campaign from the management server. Because the management server already had LDAP connectivity to Active Directory (it needs it to authenticate VPN users), the attacker used it as their launch platform for domain attacks:

  • Decrypted the LDAP service account password — the device config stores it encrypted, but with root access the attacker has the master key. They extracted it in plaintext and hardcoded it into every subsequent script.
  • Enumerated every user and group in the domain via LDAP queries.
  • Sprayed passwords against every user account using organization-themed passwords. The domain had lockoutThreshold=0 — meaning no account lockout, allowing unlimited spray attempts.
  • Attempted to create backdoor AD accounts — both a user account (tried in every OU) and a machine account (exploiting the default MachineAccountQuota setting).
  • Analyzed AD ACL chains for privilege escalation paths.
  • Attempted SAML signing key extraction from the Keycloak IdP configuration.
  • Probed Keycloak SSO for authentication bypass.

The attack results — whether the password spray found valid credentials, whether the backdoor accounts were created, whether SAML keys were extracted — stayed on the management server's local filesystem and were not among the artifacts we recovered. This means we cannot determine the full extent of the compromise.

Management Server → Active Directory

StatusActivity
✓LDAP password decrypted from config
✓Full user & group enumeration
?Password spray (all users, no lockout)
?Backdoor user + machine account creation
?SAML signing key extraction

What the Attacker Has Now

From the recovered artifacts, we can confirm the attacker possesses:

  • Persistent remote access to the organization's internal network via a boot-surviving reverse tunnel and SOCKS proxy — likely still active
  • Root webshells on two firewalls and the firewall management server — likely still active
  • The full Active Directory user and group listing — a complete organizational blueprint
  • Decrypted LDAP service account credentials — enabling direct AD queries at any time
  • Private keys harvested from the firewall filesystem — HA replication keys, SSL/TLS certificate keys, and device authentication keys
  • Complete network topology — every IP, hostname, subnet, server role, and VPN gateway
  • SAML IdP configuration with weak security settings (validate-idp-certificate: no)
  • 22 additional parked firewalls across the US, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea — ready for exploitation at any time

What we cannot determine is whether the password spray, backdoor account creation, or SAML key extraction succeeded. If any of these attacks worked, the compromise extends far beyond the perimeter firewalls into the organization's identity infrastructure.

Attribution Indicators

We do not attribute this activity to a named threat actor. However, multiple indicators point to a Chinese-nexus operation:

IndicatorDetail
Target selectionUS, Japan, Taiwan, South Korea exclusively. These are the primary strategic intelligence targets for Chinese state-aligned operations in the Pacific.
FOFAThe internet reconnaissance platform used to discover targets is a Chinese service.
ioxA Chinese-developed tunneling utility observed among the recovered tools.
DeepSeek and KimiThe LLMs configured in the aiscan offensive security platform are Chinese language models.
UTC+8 timestampsThe infrastructure's clock ran on China Standard Time, confirmed by comparing log timestamps against HTTP Date: response headers from targets.
Chinese-language promptsThe aiscan session logs contain user messages in Chinese.

Conclusion

This operation demonstrates a level of preparation and capability that sets it apart from opportunistic exploitation. The attacker invested significant effort into vulnerability research — obtaining the vendor’s firmware, decrypting it, extracting PHP libraries, building precise memory profiles for 9 different software versions, and calibrating exploit geometry through lab testing. The exploitation itself was automated and efficient: 240 targets attempted in a single batch, with version-specific profiles selected automatically.

There was a clear-cut focus on government targets.

The attacker scanned 19,000 firewalls, rooted 24, and immediately identified the two that mattered. Within hours of compromising a US government-affiliated firewall, they had tunneled into the internal network, compromised a third server using the same PHP2Shell exploit, and launched a full Active Directory attack campaign — all through a chain that started with a single unauthenticated HTTPS request to a management interface that should never have been exposed to the internet.

The 22 other rooted firewalls remain parked with active webshells. The persistent tunnel into the US government organization is likely still running. And the attacker still has 19,000 fingerprinted targets they can revisit as they develop profiles for additional OS versions.

As always, we recommend that organizations rapidly deploy relevant patches. Follow your vendor’s guidance for more information on this issue.

Closing the Gap Between Discovery and Defense

For governments and critical infrastructure, finding a vulnerability is only the beginning. Defenders need to identify exposed systems, establish what attackers can exploit, and act before a foothold becomes a wider compromise.

Dream addresses that challenge through two complementary cyberdefense platforms:

  • Sphere scales national cyber defense. It maps exposure, prioritizes risks, and detects and responds to attacks across government networks, tailored to each nation’s threats and infrastructure.
  • Hero scales cyber research. Its autonomous research agents help experts investigate threats, discover and validate vulnerabilities—including in software without source code—and develop remediation guidance and patches. This is the tool that was used by Dream researchers to conduct the investigation detailed in this post.

Together, they connect deeper investigation with defense across the national attack surface.

item.title: Zero click, silent, remote Android DoS (297 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://smsofdeath.com/, See on Hacker News

Android Telephony · Zero-Click · Remote DoS

A single malformed WAP Push SMS crashes com.android.phone on Android, dropping active calls (including emergency calls), with zero interaction from the victim.

⚠ Working proof-of-concept, authorised testing only. Read the warning & license before downloading.

Component
WapPushOverSmsframeworks/opt/telephony

Interaction
Nonezero-click, silent

Vector
Remote SMSWAP Push, port 2948

Vendor status
● Won't Fixclassified Non-Security

Reporter
Mark Blaszczykindependent

Reported
5 May 2026Android & Devices VRP

Disclosed
29 Oct 2026after 90-day timeline

CVE
Noneno CVE issued

01 / The vulnerability

An unchecked cast turns a 5-byte header into a negative array size

When Android receives a WAP Push message, WapPushOverSms.decodeWapPdu() reads the WSP header length as a uintvar. The value comes back as a long, is cast to int with no range check, and is then used directly as the size of a new byte array:

// WapPushOverSms.java:217  header length read as long, cast with no bounds check
int headerLength = (int) pduDecoder.getValue32();
    ...
// WapPushOverSms.java:244  the cast value is used as an array size
byte[] header = new byte[headerLength];

A 5-byte uintvar of 88 80 80 80 00 decodes to 0x80000000. Cast to a signed 32-bit int, that is -2147483648. Allocating new byte[-2147483648] throws an uncaught NegativeArraySizeException on the telephony main thread, killing com.android.phone:

E AndroidRuntime: FATAL EXCEPTION: main
E AndroidRuntime: Process: com.android.phone
E AndroidRuntime: java.lang.NegativeArraySizeException: -2147483648
E AndroidRuntime:   at ...WapPushOverSms.decodeWapPdu(WapPushOverSms.java:244)
E AndroidRuntime:   at ...WapPushOverSms.dispatchWapPdu(WapPushOverSms.java:339)
E AndroidRuntime:   at ...InboundSmsHandler.processMessagePart(InboundSmsHandler.java:1169)
E AndroidRuntime:   at ...InboundSmsHandler$DeliveringState.processMessage(InboundSmsHandler.java:627)

The message is delivered as a data SMS and is never shown to the user: there is nothing in the inbox, and the victim never sees the sender's number.

02 / Impact

Remote, silent, and recoverable only with effort

  • Zero-click. The victim does nothing. No tap, no open, no notification.
  • Silent. Nothing appears in Messages; the attacker's number is never shown.
  • Calls drop, including emergency calls. Active voice calls terminate with DisconnectCause CS_DEATH as the process restarts.
  • Telephony blackout. 1-2 seconds of no service per message while com.android.phone restarts.
  • Carrier redelivery amplifies it. Unacknowledged messages are re-sent by the carrier, re-crashing the phone; a single message caused intermittent outages for up to a week in testing.
  • ~20 messages render the device unusable for an extended period.
  • Persistent denial of service. Rapid repeated delivery corrupts the SQLite database behind SMS storage, turning a momentary crash into a phone that crashes on every boot (detailed below).

Tested across multiple makes and models (Pixel 9 on April 2026 firmware, various Samsung Galaxy and A-series) with a 100% reproduction rate.

From a 2-second crash to a bricked phone: the SQLite race

A single message is a repeated transient outage. Sending the payload rapidly in succession (≈30 messages) is materially worse: the crashes interleave with the telephony provider's writes to the SMS store and hit a race condition that corrupts the SQLite database holding the device's messages.

Once the database is corrupt, com.android.phone no longer needs a fresh message to fail: it crashes immediately on every boot as it reads the damaged store. The phone is now persistently without telephony, and a restart does not clear it.

Recovery is hostile, and this is the critical part: a factory reset only helps temporarily, because the carrier re-sends the unacknowledged payload and re-triggers the crash. Full recovery required:

  • Removing the physical SIM and inserting it into a non-Android device (e.g. an iPhone) so the carrier's retried messages are acknowledged and stop being redelivered;
  • Then clearing the SMS records / corrupt database over ADB.

On a device using an eSIM, where the SIM can't simply be moved to another handset, recovery would be significantly harder, and for a non-technical user, effectively out of reach.

This is the distinction the report turns on. It is not a transient crash: it is a remote, zero-click, persistent denial of service requiring a factory reset (and more) to recover, which is the exact shape of a "Destructive Remote DoS" in the VRP's own rules.

03 / Why this is serious

A remote attacker can cut a phone off from Triple Zero

Dropping calls is not an inconvenience when one of those calls is to emergency services. While a device is under this attack, or bricked by the SQLite corruption, it cannot reliably place a call to 000. The attack is remote, needs only the victim's number, and shows them nothing.

Australia treats access to emergency calling as a mandatory property of a mobile service, not a nice-to-have. Under the Telecommunications (Emergency Call Service) Determination, administered by the ACMA, carriers are required to identify mobile phones that cannot reach Triple Zero, help the customer move to a working device, and stop providing service to the affected handset. Telstra states plainly that it is required to block phones that can no longer call 000, notifying the customer and blocking the device if nothing is done within 28 days.

The consequence is perverse: the regulatory remedy for a phone that can't reach 000 is to cut it off the network, not to patch the OS. So an attacker who can remotely induce that condition on an Android handset can, in effect, get the victim's own device barred from carrier service until a fix exists. The regulation exists precisely because loss of emergency-call access is considered a public-safety failure; this bug manufactures that failure on demand.

The framework was tightened in 2024 following the 3G shutdown, which left some phones able to make ordinary calls but unable to reach emergency services, the same functional state this vulnerability produces.

Sources: ACMA: proposed amendments to the ECS Determination · Telstra: Emergency Call Service Determination · Dept. of PM&C: impact analysis

04 / The fix

One bounds check

The remedy is a range check before the cast in WapPushOverSms.java (line 217), provided to Google on the day of the first report:

long rawHeaderLen = pduDecoder.getValue32();
if (rawHeaderLen < 0 || rawHeaderLen > pdu.length) {
    result.statusCode = Intents.RESULT_SMS_GENERIC_ERROR;
    return result;
}
int headerLength = (int) rawHeaderLen;
05 / Disclosure timeline

Communication with Google

The report was filed through the Android & Google Devices VRP and resubmitted twice as a mis-triage appeal. Across three tickets and four engineers, Google classified it as a non-security issue.

Researcher Android Security Team Status change

  • 5 May 2026ResearcherReport filed: zero-click WAP Push crash in WapPushOverSms (issue 509520497). Suggested fix provided the same day.
  • 5 May 2026Android SecurityAssigned for investigation; researcher asked to follow coordinated disclosure.
  • 15 May 2026ResearcherRequests higher priority: reproduced on 5 handsets, emergency-call impact, Australian carrier regulations.
  • 20 Jun 2026Android SecurityClosed Won't Fix (Infeasible): "not a security vulnerability."
  • 20 Jun 2026ResearcherClarifies this is a remote permanent DoS; ~20 messages permanently disable the phone. Resubmits as appeal (issues 525810560 and 525816147, "SMS of DEATH").
  • 20 Jun 2026Android SecurityResubmit 525810560 closed within 3 minutes Won't Fix (Not Reproducible).
  • 22 Jun 2026ResearcherReports SQLite corruption from rapid sends → crash on boot; recovery needs SIM swap to a non-Android device + ADB.
  • 23 Jun 2026Android SecurityRequests disclosure plans; reminds of the 90-day VRP timeline and asks to review any write-up in advance.
  • 23 Jun 2026ResearcherAgrees to hold for public safety; offers to brief Australian carriers so they can schedule a block. Restates the one-line fix.
  • 2-3 Jul 2026Android SecurityAppeal marked Duplicate of the original; re-evaluation confirms same root cause.
  • 16 Jul 2026Android SecurityOriginal reopened after the issue surfaced on Discord, then confirmed a duplicate again.
  • 16 Jul 2026ResearcherAdds detail: the behaviour meets the VRP's own "Destructive Remote DoS" criterion.
  • 17 Jul 2026Android SecurityAcknowledges the extra context; triage to take another look: "4 engineers will have evaluated the report."
  • 27 Oct 2026ResearcherRequests a status update after three months of silence.
  • 29 Oct 2026Android SecurityFinal decision: Won't Fix, quoting "does not meet the severity threshold ... considered a Non-Security Issue (NSI)."

Why this is public. The issue was reported privately and held well beyond the VRP's 90-day window. Google declined to fix it across three tickets and four engineers, classifying a remote, zero-click, emergency-call-dropping denial of service as a non-security issue. Full disclosure follows so that users, carriers and downstream OEMs can assess the risk and mitigate.

06 / Proof of concept

Source & APK

The proof-of-concept Android app and full source code are published on GitHub. The app crafts the malformed WAP Push PDU and sends it as a data SMS to a target number.

Warning: this is a working weapon. The repository contains a proof-of-concept that can remotely disrupt and brick mobile phones. It is published strictly for security research, education, and defensive testing.

Only run it against devices you own or are explicitly authorised to test. Using it against anyone else is a crime, and interfering with a person's ability to reach emergency services (000) is a serious criminal offence in Australia and most countries.

The software is provided "as is", with no warranty, under the Apache License 2.0. The author accepts no liability for any use, misuse, or damage. By downloading the APK or the source, you accept full responsibility for what you do with it.

item.title: Forging a Microsoft Edge Full Chain with Logic Bugs Only (221 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://blog.orange.tw/posts/2026-10-the-last-proof-of-human-craft-browser-full-chain/, See on Hacker News

I think I should still dump some of my work once in a while, even though it feels like fewer and fewer people actually sit down and read articles these days (or maybe now they all leave it to their agents XD). Anyway, this is what I built for Pwn2Own Berlin 2026 — a completely handmade, logic-only Microsoft Edge Full Chain, with no memory corruption, and no AI at all! 🔥

Confirmed! Orange Tsai (@orange_8361) of DEVCORE Research Team (@d3vc0r3) chained 4 logic bugs to achieve a sandbox escape on Microsoft Edge, earning $175,000 and 17.5 Master of Pwn points. Full win! #Pwn2Own #P2OBerlin https://t.co/vJaIpGG4cD

— TrendAI Zero Day Initiative (@thezdi) May 14, 2026

The whole chain is made up of five bugs and two Windows features. I have also shared the whole bug-hunting and chaining process at this year’s HITCON and Hexacon, plus some fun stories along the way. You can check the slides here!

Also, maybe everyone thinks LLMs can already pwn everything in the AI era, so something made entirely by hand somehow feels a bit more precious. That might also be why this chain was nominated for this year’s Pwnie Awards and won the Epic Achievement award. 🎉

Let’s Navigate!

So where do we start with a logic-only full chain? Well, since it’s a “browser,” let’s start by looking at how “browsing” (or what Chromium calls “navigation”) works. I won’t go into too much detail in this post, because I think in this era, you can just ask your agents to fill in the details :)

But I’d still recommend reading “Life of a Navigation“ from Chrome University if you want to get the full picture.

The Forgotten Navigation Throttles

While I was walking through the Chromium Navigation flow, something called “Navigation Throttles” caught my attention. They live in the Browser Process, and intercept all navigation requests initiated by either the Browser or the Renderer. Maybe it’s easy to say this in hindsight, but out of the 3,000+ CVEs Google Chrome has fixed over the past five years, there are only fewer than 20 related to them. So I guess this is also a corner not too many people pay attention to.

Anyway, I started digging into the Navigation Throttles, and checked how Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge implemented them. And while going through the code, I found that Edge has a throttle called EdgeCAGuidanceNavigationThrottle for its enterprise Entra ID feature (the CA here stands for Conditional Access). The purpose of this throttle is to guide users to the right User Profile when Edge detects them signing in with a work account on a Microsoft website. And to fire this throttle, you have to start a navigation from a specific Microsoft-owned origin, such as login.live.com:

And once the throttle is fired, Edge would compare the email of the current User Profile with ?email={email}. If they don’t match, Edge pops up a dialog guiding you to switch accounts.

But if they do match, Edge would then grab the URL you were originally heading to from switch_profile={url}, and launch a new navigation with Chromium’s internal Navigation API:

So basically, the throttle cancels the original navigation when the target URL matches a specific internal format, and then launches a new one with the URL from the attacker-controlled Query String, if the conditions are met. Since this new navigation is initiated by the Browser Process, in theory we can do a few things we couldn’t do before, such as jumping to normally prohibited pages like edge://settings or devtools://..., or even pseudo-schemes like javascript:alert(origin).

Though the JavaScript pseudo-scheme sounds like a powerful primitive, you still need to obtain the Execution Context on login.live.com to fire the throttle in the first place. So being able to jump to javascript: doesn’t really give you any extra capability. At most, it’s just like a Self-XSS, or a way to turn an Open Redirect there into XSS. Either way, you’re still only executing JavaScript in the same login.live.com context.

Honestly, I didn’t take this bug too seriously at first glance. To me, it was just a stronger Open Redirect that could jump to a few more Browser-Level Schemes, and still needed to be chained with other bugs. So the bug just sat in my notes for weeks… 🤦‍♂️

Sourceless Navigation: A New UXSS Primitive

The turning point was when I was going over the Chromium architecture one day and started thinking: The throttle is handled in the Browser Process, so the new navigation is initiated from the browser as well. However, the page we fired the throttle from, login.live.com, lives in the Renderer, and while investigating the logic, I couldn’t find any code tying the Browser and Renderer together. So… CURRENT_TAB refers to which tab, exactly?

To find this out, I ran a quick test and added a delay to the original trigger:

And during the delay, we manually switched the Edge to a new tab to see what would happen, and…

Boom! We got a UXSS on google.com, and that’s also the first bug of the whole chain. To fully understand the UXSS root cause, we dug into Chromium’s source code. We found that if Navigate() is called without specifying the source_contents (the Renderer source to bind to), Chromium would use the current active tab as the Renderer source automatically.

↓ Path: chromium/chrome/browser/ui/browser_navigator.cc

Though the code path requires params.disposition to be CURRENT_TAB and params.source_contents to be NULL, luckily, those are the defaults, so even Chromium’s own example code gets this wrong. I guess this should count as a new UXSS attack surface!

The 0-Click Challenges

The UXSS primitive we just got sounds great, but firing that still comes with quite a few challenges in practice. Here we list four we faced while weaponizing the UXSS, and how we cracked them with more and more bugs 😉.

1. The Throttle Must Be Fired from a Trusted Origin

The first challenge, as we mentioned earlier: this UXSS has to be fired from certain Microsoft sites. Though we could still find an XSS there to make that happen, that sounds like a painful job, so we’d keep it as a last resort. Instead, we decided to see if there was any low-hanging fruit in the origin check first.

We found that EdgeCAGuidanceNavigationThrottle uses GetLastCommittedURL() to retrieve the origin that fired the navigation, and then check it. At first glance, this looks like the correct way to do the validation. But take a second look, and you’ll notice Microsoft seems to have forgotten that a navigation can come not just from the current WebContents, but also from another window… So a simple window.open(...) is enough to bypass it!

↓ You can run this on any website to fire the throttle

So far, we can bypass the origin check with a cross-window navigation. However, modern browsers don’t let webpages open new windows that easily nowadays, so here comes another new problem: the Popup Blocker would block window.open(...) by default.

To crack this, we kept reversing Microsoft Edge. And we found Microsoft, maybe for internal use, made its own hardcoded whitelist for popups… So a popup like the following would normally be blocked as expected:

But if you swap the URL for the whitelisted one… the window just appears. And then remember to navigate it back to the original site, and you’ve bypassed the Popup Blocker!

Thank you, Microsoft!

3. The Need for a Signed-In Profile

Now that we can fire EdgeCAGuidanceNavigationThrottle from wherever we want, the next step is to get past the Conditional Access checks. The code first requires Microsoft Edge to already have a signed-in User Profile, and then checks if ?email={email} matches the profile’s email. Both conditions have to be met before we reach the sourceless, browser-initiated navigation to finally trigger our UXSS primitive.

However, since we can’t assume the target environment has a signed-in profile in advance, we still need to find a way to make the attack work even if it doesn’t. While exploring Microsoft Edge, we came across a great feature called “OneAuth”. The feature lets any Edge WebView application automatically sign in with your current MSA credentials when visiting Microsoft-owned sites. And it turns out that starting with 25H2, Windows OOBE requires you to sign in with an MSA (unless you use the local-account workaround). So even if you’ve never created a User Profile in the browser, just visiting www.microsoft.com is enough for Edge to create one and sign you in automatically.

Thanks again, Microsoft!


4. The Need for Prior Knowledge of the Login Email

With the sign-in issue cracked, the last challenge is to get the victim’s email in advance. Of course, we could try some social engineering, or keep reversing Microsoft Edge to find another bug that leaks that for us. But since the automatic sign-in already sets several Microsoft cookies, we thought Web Hacking would be an easier way to steal the email. So we fired up Burp Suite and started looking for web vulnerabilities.

We spent a few hours and found several XSS bugs on Microsoft sites. While poking around, I noticed that assets.msn.com, which is embedded in edge://new-tab-page-online, returns the currently signed-in user’s email. And even more interesting, when I checked the response header, the site seemed to have a CORS misconfiguration…

So with a simple fetch(...) with credentials included, you can easily grab any Microsoft Edge user’s email from any website:

Putting It All Together!

So far, to make this primitive work, we’ve chained together:

  • A Trusted Origin bypass caused by a missing cross-window Opener check
  • A Popup Blocker bypass caused by a hardcoded whitelist
  • A OneAuth feature that automatically signs you in
  • A CORS misconfiguration that lets us steal the signed-in user’s email

Now we can finally trigger the UXSS without a single click! And even better, since this UXSS is initiated from the Browser Process (HandleRendererDebugURL in Mojo, if you’re interested), it can ignore any CSP entirely. That means we can run JavaScript on google.com, facebook.com, icloud.com, or whatever website we want!

Breaking Out of the Browser Sandbox

So we have a Universal XSS. Does it mean that we can do whatever we want? If we’re talking about Web Security, then yes. But our goal here is to get ACE (Arbitrary Code Execution), so UXSS alone is far from enough. And we still need to find a way to break out of the Browser Sandbox to turn this UXSS into code execution.

The first and most straightforward idea that came to my mind was: since we can run JavaScript on any website, or more precisely, any origin, why not just leverage privileged WebUI pages like edge://settings or edge://downloads to get ACE?

This naive approach was of course already mitigated by the Chromium developers. In the Renderer’s Mojo handler, there’s an extra check: if the origin belongs to one of the following privileged WebUIs, the Renderer simply ignores the JavaScript URL.

↓ Path: chromium/third_party/blink/renderer/core/frame/local_frame.cc

↓ Path: chromium/third_party/blink/renderer/platform/weborigin/scheme_registry.cc

Basically, Chromium has put every privileged WebUI you can think of on the not_allowing_javascript_urls_schemes blacklist. So at that point, I still got stuck for a long while. 😖

Arbitrary File Write via Immersive Reader

However, as we continued exploring Microsoft Edge, we found that Edge had its own Reading Mode called Immersive Reader. And unlike Chrome’s built-in Reading Mode, Immersive Reader seems to have been forked from Chromium early on, with Microsoft building on top of it. So instead of the old chrome-distiller:// or the blacklisted chrome-untrusted://, Edge uses a custom read:// scheme. And Microsoft seems to have forgotten to add this scheme to the blacklist as well, so our UXSS works on this privileged WebUI :)

Starting from this privileged WebUI, we can access lots of native C++ objects through JavaScript. And one of them called chrome.edgeFeedbackPrivate.zipDiagnosticLogFiles() looked particularly interesting to me. We tried it out, and found that the function takes two parameters, a filename and a JSON string:

↓ We ran this on read://https_orange.tw/?url=https://orange.tw

While playing with it, we observed that Microsoft Edge would first create a temporary folder and write AAAAAAAA to the file ORANGE.json. It would then pack the whole folder into LOL.ZIP, upload it to a Microsoft server, and clean everything up afterward. Of course, you’d want to try ../… Yes, it does let you escape the temporary folder. But that .json extension is still a bit annoying. Maybe you’re also wondering if a NULL Byte could get rid of it… Of course it can! So now we have an arbitrary file write that can control both the filename and the content, and we can overwrite any file anywhere we want!

Thank you again and again, Microsoft!


Overwriting protocols.json to Auto-Launch Protocol Handlers

Now, we’ve got almost all the pieces. The last step is figuring out how to turn a browser-level arbitrary file write into ACE to complete the chain. We observed that Microsoft Edge would do some interesting side-loading while initializing, such as reading a bunch of config files or loading DLLs from a writable folder.

So the DLL side-loading sounds juicy. However, since our file write is wrapped in JSON, the content has to be a valid UTF-8 string. And because Microsoft Edge is a 64-bit process, we’d have to drop a 64-bit DLL, too. After spending some time working on this, we found that we couldn’t construct a valid 64-bit PE header that met the UTF-8 requirement in any case, so we gave up on DLL side-loading.

We ended up solving this in a less obvious way. We found that besides OneAuth, Edge also loads a bunch of components while initializing, and one of them is “AutoLaunchProtocolsComponent”. The component would read a configuration file called protocols.json from a folder we can write to, and that file defines which origins are allowed to launch which URL protocol handlers. So by overwriting the file, we can launch any protocol handler from any origin.

↓ Path: AppData\Local\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\AutoLaunchProtocolsComponent\1.0.0.10\protocols.json

As for how do we get Microsoft Edge to re-initialize? Just use our earlier browser-initiated navigation to jump to edge://restart! :)

From telnet:// to Code Execution!

Here we chose telnet:// to get code execution. On Windows, the telnet handler would try to invoke telnet.exe, but the binary isn’t shipped by default, so Windows goes looking for it in the directories listed in the PATH environment variable. And one of those directories just happens to be writable by us…

So by simply dropping a modified protocols.json and a 32-bit tiny PE, we got ACE. The whole exploit is less than 100 lines of code. The restart isn’t really necessary in a real attack, only for Pwn2Own. Let’s check out the demo! 🔥


Final Thoughts

From zero experience with modern browser exploitation to completing the full chain, the whole research took me two full months, with no LLMs/AI involved at all. But why, you might ask? Perhaps because it sounds cool, or maybe it was also just good timing — I only started using coding agents like Codex and Claude Code around March this year, and by then, I’d already found all the bugs and done the hard part ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

So what’s the hard part? For memory corruption, it’s often the exploitation. But we’re playing with logic bugs, where the hard part is finding them, and once you find them all, chaining is the easiest part. So that’s also why I kept the whole exploit AI-free.

Apart from that, I also see the UXSS primitive as a new attack surface, and agree that in the AI era, “Attack Surface is the new 0day“. I wanted to explore this gold mine more before sharing it with the AI giants. That’s another reason why I decided not to use AI on this chain.

Of course, I’m not some old-fashioned guy who refuses to try new things, either. Outside of this chain, I’m also tokenmaxxing and addicted to AI. I believe once you’ve tasted how convenient LLMs are, no one would want to go back to hunting bugs by hand. That’s also the future, I think.

I’m also not that afraid of being replaced by AI.
